countries.name: Spain
countries.tagline: The world's largest vineyard, from Atlantic Albariño to slate-grown Priorat and the flor-veiled bodegas of Jerez.

stats.note: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (published 2026): 919 kha of vineyard (all uses), the world's largest, 13.1% of the total; 28.7 mhl of wine; exports 19.6 mhl worth 3.0 bn EUR. Spain's own wine-market observatory counted 889,470 ha of wine-grape vineyard in 2025.

countries.overview:
Spain has more land under vine than any other country on earth. The OIV counted 919,000 hectares in 2025, about 13 percent of the world's vineyard, ahead of France and China. Yet in most years Spain makes less wine than either Italy or France: 28.7 million hectolitres in 2025, third in the world. That gap between area and output is the first thing to understand about Spanish wine. Much of the vineyard sits on the hot, dry Meseta, the high central plateau, where old bush vines planted wide apart on poor soils give small crops with little or no irrigation. A Spanish hectare is often a tough, sparse, beautiful thing.

The second thing is the extraordinary range packed inside one country. In the far northwest, Galicia is green, wet and granitic, a land of Albariño trained on stone pergolas and Mencía clinging to Roman-era terraces above the Sil. Two hours east, Rioja and Ribera del Duero make the country's most famous reds from Tempranillo, one shaped by the Ebro and the Atlantic air that slips through the Sierra de Cantabria, the other by a plateau nearly 800 metres up where summer nights turn cold. Catalonia gives the world Cava and the black slate of Priorat. The Levante coast grows Monastrell and Bobal in near-desert conditions. Andalusia keeps the strangest and most profound wines of all: Sherry, aged under a living veil of yeast in cathedral-like bodegas cooled by Atlantic winds, and the raisined Pedro Ximénez of Montilla and Málaga. Out in the Atlantic, the Canary Islands still grow ungrafted vines in volcanic ash, a living museum of what European vineyards looked like before phylloxera.

History explains much of this. Phoenicians brought the vine to Gadir, today's Cádiz, almost three thousand years ago. Rome made Hispania a great exporter. The English thirst for Sherry, Canary and Málaga ran for four centuries, and English, Irish and Scottish merchant families still give their names to Jerez bodegas. When phylloxera wrecked France in the 1870s and 1880s, Bordeaux buyers came south, and Rioja learned to age wine in 225-litre barricas. Then phylloxera reached Spain too, and the 20th century brought civil war, autarky under Franco and a cooperative system built for volume. Modern fine wine in Spain is younger than people think: most of the estates that define it today were founded or reinvented after 1980.

The last forty years have been a revolution in fits and starts. Spain joined the European Community in 1986. Ribera del Duero rose from almost nothing to rival Rioja. A handful of idealists rebuilt Priorat from abandoned terraces in 1989. Galician and Canarian growers rescued native varieties that had nearly vanished. A new generation in Gredos, Bierzo, Ribeira Sacra and the Canaries began making fresh, transparent wines from old Garnacha, Mencía and Listán Negro. The rules followed the wines: since 2017 Rioja, Priorat, Bierzo and Cava have all built place-based hierarchies of villages and single vineyards, a quiet move away from Spain's old habit of judging wine mainly by how long it spent in oak.

Spain today has 106 protected designations of origin for wine (DOPs) and 43 protected geographical indications, according to the Ministry of Agriculture's register of July 2026. The giant of the system is La Mancha, with about 147,000 registered hectares; Rioja leads by value, earning roughly a quarter of the money made by all Spanish DOP wine. Domestic drinking has fallen for decades, and the vineyard is shrinking: the ministry's market observatory counted 889,470 hectares of wine grapes in 2025, the first time below 900,000, after losing nearly half its area since 1980. Spain sells more wine abroad by volume than almost anyone (19.6 million hectolitres in 2025, second only to Italy), much of it in bulk, which is why its average export price lags far behind France and Italy. The country's challenge, and its opportunity, is to be paid for the quality that its old vines and wild landscapes can give.

history.title: Phoenicians at Gadir
history.text: Traders from Tyre founded Gadir (Cádiz) on an island at the edge of the known world; ancient writers dated it to 1104 BC, archaeology to the 9th and 8th centuries BC. They brought vines, amphorae and the habit of trading wine. Across the bay, the Phoenician town at Castillo de Doña Blanca later had a stone winepress, among the oldest found in Iberia, a direct ancestor of the Sherry country around it.

history.title: Iberians press wine at Benimaquia
history.text: On a hilltop above Dénia, the Iberian settlement of Alt de Benimaquia had plaster-lined treading floors and tanks for making wine, together with local amphorae. It shows that native Iberians, not only colonists, were making wine on the Levante coast centuries before Rome, the same coast that now grows Moscatel and Monastrell.

history.title: Hispania feeds Rome
history.text: Roman Hispania shipped wine from Tarraconensis, especially the Laietanian coast near Barcelona, in amphorae found across Gaul and Italy, and Pliny praised the wines of Tarraco and Lauro. Baetica (Andalusia) was the empire's great olive-oil exporter: Rome's Monte Testaccio is a hill built from around 53 million broken Baetican oil amphorae, not wine jars, a common confusion. Columella, the great Roman writer on vine growing, was born in Gades.

history.title: Al-Andalus and Sherish
history.text: Under Muslim rule the vineyards survived, used for raisins, grape syrups and, discreetly, wine, which court poets in Córdoba and Seville celebrated. Jerez was called Sherish, the root of the word Sherry. After Alfonso X took Jerez in 1264, Castilian kings encouraged planting, and by the 15th century Jerez wine was already reaching English and Flemish ports.

history.title: Carthusians found Scala Dei
history.text: Monks from Provence founded the Carthusian priory of Scala Dei below the Montsant cliffs, and for six centuries they ruled and planted the slate hills that took the name Priorat, the land of the prior. Monasteries did the same across Spain, from the Cistercians of Poblet and Veruela to the Benedictines of the Ribeira Sacra.

history.title: Drake sacks Cádiz and sack becomes fashionable
history.text: Francis Drake's raid on Cádiz carried off about 2,900 barrels of Jerez wine meant for the Spanish fleet. The plunder helped make sack, as the English called the strong wines of Jerez, the Canaries and Málaga, a London craze; Shakespeare's Falstaff praises sherris-sack at length in Henry IV, Part 2. For the next three centuries English demand shaped what Andalusia made.

history.title: Canary sack
history.text: Sweet Malvasía from Tenerife and La Palma was one of the most prized wines in England and its colonies, shipped from ports such as Garachico. Trade disputes, the rise of Madeira and Port, and a 1706 eruption that buried Garachico's harbour ended the boom, but the islands kept their vines, and later escaped phylloxera.

history.title: Bordeaux methods and the first Cava
history.text: Luciano de Murrieta made Bordeaux-style aged wine in Rioja from 1852, and the Marqués de Riscal built his Elciego bodega in 1858 with a French winemaker and barrels. Eloy Lecanda founded Vega Sicilia in 1864 with Bordeaux vines. In 1872 Josep Raventós of Codorníu made Spain's first traditional-method sparkling wine in Sant Sadurní d'Anoia: modern Spanish fine wine starts in these two decades.

history.title: Phylloxera arrives late
history.text: While phylloxera ruined France, Bordeaux merchants bought Spanish wine by the trainload, and Haro's railway station, opened in 1863, became the heart of a boom. The louse was found near Málaga in 1878 and spread north, reaching Rioja around 1900. Replanting on American rootstocks, and the end of French demand, left many regions poorer and drove growers into cooperatives.

history.title: Rioja's Consejo and the Estatuto del Vino
history.text: Rioja formed Spain's first Consejo Regulador to defend its name, created by royal decree in 1925 and constituted in 1926. In 1932 the Republic's Estatuto del Vino set up a national system of denominaciones de origen and named the first ones, among them Jerez, Málaga and Rioja. Civil war (1936 to 1939) interrupted almost everything.

history.title: Cooperatives and the 1970 wine law
history.text: Under Franco, state policy pushed farmers into cooperatives built for volume, and by the 1970s they made most Spanish wine, much of it sold in bulk. The 1970 Estatuto de la Viña, del Vino y de los Alcoholes modernised the DO framework and created a national institute to oversee it. Many cooperatives later became the base of modern quality, from Priorat to Utiel-Requena.

history.title: Europe, Ribera and the Priorat revolution
history.text: Spain joined the European Community in 1986. Ribera del Duero, a DO only since 1982, became a star. In 1989 René Barbier, Álvaro Palacios, Daphne Glorian, Josep Lluís Pérez and Carles Pastrana shared their first harvest in Gratallops, reviving Priorat. Rioja became Spain's first DOCa in 1991; Priorat won the Catalan equivalent, DOQ, in 2000, confirmed nationally in 2009.

history.title: The Ley de la Viña y del Vino and Vinos de Pago
history.text: Law 24/2003 set today's pyramid, adding the Vino de Calidad con Indicación Geográfica and the Vino de Pago, a single estate with its own DO. Carlos Falcó's Dominio de Valdepusa, near Toledo, became the first pago. By 2026 there were 28, most in Castilla-La Mancha, Navarra and Valencia.

history.title: Spain discovers the vineyard
history.text: A wave of place-based rules: Rioja's viñedos singulares and zone and village labels from 2017, Priorat's paratges and classified vineyards from 2017, Bierzo's village and paraje wines from 2019, Cava's zoning and Paraje Calificado tier, and Sherry's 2021 reforms allowing unfortified wines and pago names. At the same time, growers who wanted stricter rules left: Corpinnat walked out of Cava in 2019, and DO Penedès went fully organic from the 2025 harvest.

countries.classification:
Spain's pyramid runs from plain *vino* (no origin beyond Spain) through 43 IGPs, still widely labelled *Vino de la Tierra*, to the protected designations of origin (DOPs). Within the DOPs, the 2003 wine law created several rungs. A *Vino de Calidad con Indicación Geográfica* (VC) is the entry step, meant as a waiting room for a future DO; there were seven in 2026, among them Islas Canarias, Cangas, Lebrija and Cebreros. The *Denominación de Origen* (DO) is the core of the system, with around 70. A *Denominación de Origen Calificada* (DOCa; DOQ in Catalan) needs at least ten years as a DO, higher prices, bottling in the zone and tighter controls: only Rioja (1991) and Priorat (DOQ 2000, national 2009) qualify. A *Vino de Pago* is a single estate with its own DOP, recognised for a distinct microclimate and soil; the winery must make and bottle the wine itself. If the pago lies inside a DOCa it may become a *Vino de Pago Calificado*. The Ministry of Agriculture's list of July 2026 counts 2 DOCa, 70 DO and 27 Vinos de Pago, plus Urbezo, an Aragonese pago registered by the EU in October 2024 but listed under the DO term, so 28 pagos in all.

Spanish labels traditionally talk more about time than place. The national ageing terms are: *joven* (young, little or no oak); *crianza* (red at least 24 months with 6 in oak; white and rosé 18 months with 6 in oak); *reserva* (red 36 months with at least 12 in oak; white and rosé 24 months with 6 in oak); and *gran reserva* (red 60 months with at least 18 in oak; white and rosé 48 months with 6 in oak). Many DOs are stricter: Rioja and Ribera del Duero demand 12 months of barrel for crianza, and Rioja asks 24 for a red gran reserva. *Roble* (oak) is a widely used informal term for a red with a few months in barrel, regulated by some DOs but not by national law. Older terms such as *noble*, *añejo* and *viejo* survive for oxidative and fortified wines. Sherry, Montilla and Málaga have their own systems, built on soleras rather than vintages.

The recent change is a turn toward the vineyard. Rioja now labels zones, villages (*vino de pueblo*) and *viñedos singulares*; Priorat stacks *vi de vila*, *vi de paratge*, *vinya classificada* and *gran vinya classificada*; Bierzo copies Burgundy with *vino de villa*, *vino de paraje* and classified vineyards; Cava splits into zones and a *Paraje Calificado* summit; Jerez can now print the name of its historic pagos. For drinkers, it means that the name of a village or a slope on a Spanish label is increasingly a promise, not just decoration.
countries.climate_soils:
Spain is the second most mountainous country in Europe, and altitude is the key to its wine. The Meseta, the plateau that covers the centre, averages around 600 to 700 metres; Ribera del Duero's vineyards rise above 900 metres, and some in Gredos, Manchuela or the Canaries go well above 1,000. Height gives cold nights and keeps acidity in grapes that bake by day. The climate is continental in the interior, with hot dry summers, harsh winters and very little rain; Mediterranean on the east and south coasts; and Atlantic in Galicia, Asturias and the Basque Country, where rainfall can pass 1,500 mm and the challenge is rot, not drought.

Rivers organise the map. The Ebro carves Rioja, Navarra and Aragón; the Duero runs west from Soria through Ribera, Rueda and Toro to the Arribes gorge and Portugal's Douro; the Miño and Sil cut the slate and granite canyons of Galicia; the Guadalquivir reaches the Atlantic at Sanlúcar, where Manzanilla is made. Mountain ranges block or channel the winds: the Sierra de Cantabria shelters Rioja from the north, and the Montsant cliffs frame Priorat.

The soils are as varied as the climates. Galicia sits on granite and slate; Bierzo and Ribeira Sacra on slate and schist; Priorat on its famous *llicorella*, a crumbling black and brown slate. Rioja and Ribera have clay-limestone and alluvial terraces; Rueda and Toro gravelly sandy soils; La Mancha red clay over limestone. Jerez has *albariza*, a brilliant white chalky marl that soaks up winter rain and feeds the vines through summer drought. In Lanzarote and parts of Tenerife and La Palma, vines root through black volcanic ash. Sandy soils in Toro, Rueda, Jumilla, Valencia and the Canaries kept phylloxera at bay, which is why Spain still has many ungrafted, pre-phylloxera vines.

Climate change is now the defining pressure. Harvests come earlier, drought years (2022 and 2023 were severe in Catalonia and Andalusia) cut yields, and growers are moving vineyards uphill, reviving drought-hardy natives and replanting bush vines. In Jerez the heat has a curious upside: musts now reach the 15 percent needed for flor wines without fortification, the logic behind the 2021 reforms.

grapes.name: Tempranillo
grapes.note: Spain's signature red and, neck and neck with Airén, its most planted variety; known as Tinto Fino or Tinta del País in Ribera del Duero, Tinta de Toro in Toro, Cencibel in La Mancha and Valdepeñas, Ull de Llebre in Catalonia. Early ripening (temprano means early), it gives cherry fruit, leather and tobacco with age.

grapes.name: Airén
grapes.note: A drought-proof white of La Mancha planted over huge areas; long the world's most planted grape by area, used for neutral whites, bulk wine and brandy.

grapes.name: Garnacha
grapes.note: Probably Aragonese in origin. The backbone of Priorat, Campo de Borja, Calatayud, Navarra rosado, Rioja Oriental and the granite heights of Gredos, where it gives perfumed, translucent reds.

grapes.name: Monastrell
grapes.note: Mourvèdre in France; the great red of the dry southeast, Jumilla, Yecla, Bullas and Alicante, and the base of Alicante's Fondillón.

grapes.name: Bobal
grapes.note: Thick-skinned red of Utiel-Requena and Manchuela, once a bulk-blending grape, now made into fresh, dark wines from old bush vines.

grapes.name: Mencía
grapes.note: The red of Bierzo, Ribeira Sacra, Valdeorras and Monterrei: floral, peppery, mineral on slate. Genetically identical to Portugal's Jaen.

grapes.name: Albariño
grapes.note: Galicia's aromatic white, about nine-tenths of the Rías Baixas vineyard; Alvarinho across the Miño in Portugal.

grapes.name: Verdejo
grapes.note: The white of Rueda, grassy and slightly bitter-almond in style, saved from oxidative-wine obscurity in the 1970s.

grapes.name: Godello
grapes.note: Galician white revived from a few vines in Valdeorras in the 1970s; also important in Bierzo. Textured, citrus and stony.

grapes.name: Palomino Fino
grapes.note: The neutral white grape behind almost all Sherry and Manzanilla; its lack of strong fruit lets flor and solera speak.

grapes.name: Pedro Ximénez
grapes.note: The white of Montilla-Moriles, also used in Jerez and Málaga; sun-dried for intensely sweet PX, or made dry and naturally strong in Montilla.

grapes.name: Macabeo (Viura), Xarel·lo and Parellada
grapes.note: The classic trio of Cava. Viura is also Rioja's main white; Xarel·lo is Penedès's pride, ageworthy and increasingly bottled alone.

grapes.name: Cariñena (Mazuelo, Samsó)
grapes.note: Named after the Aragonese town; vital to old-vine Priorat and Montsant, and a sharpening partner to Tempranillo in Rioja.

grapes.name: Graciano
grapes.note: Low-yielding, aromatic Rioja red that adds acidity and colour to Tempranillo blends.

grapes.name: Listán Negro and Listán Blanco
grapes.note: Canary Island workhorses, often grown ungrafted on volcanic soils; Listán Blanco is genetically Palomino.

grapes.name: Moscatel de Alejandría
grapes.note: Muscat of Alexandria: the sweet wines of Málaga, Valencia, Alicante's Marina Alta and Jerez's Chipiona.

regions.name: Rioja
regions.tagline: Spain's most famous red, aged in American and French oak along the Ebro and sheltered by the Sierra de Cantabria.
regions.summary:
Rioja is the name most people know, and for good reason. It is Spain's oldest regulated wine region, its first DOCa (1991) and, by value, its biggest: the Ministry of Agriculture puts its share at about 27 percent of the money earned by all Spanish DOP wine. In 2026 the DOCa had 66,500 registered hectares, 12,704 growers and 719 wineries, spread across three autonomous communities: La Rioja itself, Álava in the Basque Country, and a slice of Navarra, plus a tiny enclave of Burgos. The region follows the Ebro for about 120 km, from the narrows of the Conchas de Haro in the northwest to Alfaro in the southeast.

Rioja's classic style was born in the second half of the 19th century, when Luciano de Murrieta and the Marqués de Riscal brought Bordeaux techniques home and French merchants, desperate for wine after phylloxera, flooded in. They left behind the 225-litre barrica and the habit of long ageing, usually in American oak, which gives the classic dill, coconut and vanilla note. A traditional Gran Reserva from López de Heredia or La Rioja Alta, pale brick and smelling of dried cherries, leather and forest floor, is one of the great old-world styles.

Since the 1990s Rioja has also become a place of argument about place. Modern producers such as Artadi, Roda, Remírez de Ganuza and Contino pushed for riper fruit and French oak; others, led by Telmo Rodríguez and the growers of Rioja Alavesa, argued that Rioja should be labelled by village and vineyard rather than by months in barrel. The 2017 reform answered them partly, with zone names, village wines and *viñedos singulares*. The argument went as far as a secession attempt: some 40 Alavesa wineries sought a separate Basque DO, *Arabako Mahastiak / Viñedos de Álava*, which the Basque high court annulled in November 2024.
regions.history:
Wine was made here in Roman times, and the monasteries of San Millán de la Cogolla, where the first written words in Castilian (and Basque) appear in 10th and 11th century glosses, kept vineyards through the Middle Ages. A 1102 charter from the king of Navarre and Aragón is often cited as the first legal protection of Rioja's vineyards, and by the early modern period Logroño and Haro had ordinances controlling which wine could enter town.

The modern story begins in the 1850s. Luciano de Murrieta, trained in Bordeaux, made the first aged Rioja for export in 1852 and founded his bodega at Ygay in 1872. Camilo Hurtado de Amézaga, the Marqués de Riscal, built his Elciego winery in 1858 with Bordeaux-trained help. The railway reached Haro in 1863, and when phylloxera devastated France, Haro's Barrio de la Estación filled with bodegas shipping wine north: CVNE (1879), López de Heredia (1877), La Rioja Alta (1890), Bodegas Bilbaínas (1901). Phylloxera arrived in Rioja around 1899 to 1901 and the French went home, but the barrels and the cellar habits stayed.

A royal decree defined the area in 1902; the Consejo Regulador, the first in Spain, was created in 1925 and constituted in 1926, and Rioja celebrated its centenary in 2025 and 2026. It became Spain's first DOCa in 1991, with stricter controls and compulsory bottling in the zone. The 2017 reform introduced *vinos de zona*, *vinos de municipio* (renamed *vino de pueblo* in 2022, with 144 municipalities eligible) and *viñedos singulares*: by September 2026 the ministry had recognised 167 single vineyards, 91 in La Rioja, 73 in Álava and 3 in Navarra, covering about 270 hectares from 101 wineries. White wines, about a tenth of the vineyard after doubling in twenty years, and traditional-method sparkling wines (*Espumoso de Calidad de Rioja*, with a *Gran Añada* top tier) have joined the reds.
regions.terroir:
Two mountain chains shape Rioja. To the north the Sierra de Cantabria and the Montes Obarenes, rising to about 1,400 m, block the cold wet winds from the Bay of Biscay; to the south the Sierra de la Demanda and the Sierra de Cameros send down cool tributaries, seven of them, from the Oja (which gave Rioja its name, Río Oja) to the Najerilla, Iregua, Leza, Cidacos and Alhama. Between them the Ebro valley slopes down from about 700 m in the west to under 300 m at Alfaro, and the climate shifts from Atlantic to Mediterranean along the way.

Rioja Alta, on the western and southern banks around Haro, Briones, Cenicero and Najera, is the coolest, with clay-limestone and ferrous clay soils and alluvial terraces; it gives the finest, longest-lived classic wines. Rioja Alavesa, on the north bank in Álava below the Sierra de Cantabria, has the region's best chalky clay-limestone soils on steep terraces at 400 to 700 m, and makes perfumed, fresh Tempranillo; it is also the home of *maceración carbónica* young wines, the traditional cosechero style. Rioja Oriental (called Rioja Baja until 2018) is warmer and drier, with alluvial and clay soils, where Garnacha does well, especially on the slopes of Monte Yerga and near Alfaro. Vineyards in all three zones now climb higher in search of freshness: a label may say *viñedo de altura* only from 550 m up.
regions.grapes: Tempranillo dominates, about 88 percent of red plantings. It is blended with Garnacha (body and warmth, especially from Rioja Oriental), Mazuelo (Cariñena, for acidity and tannin), Graciano (perfume and acidity, a Rioja treasure) and Maturana Tinta. Whites are led by Viura (Macabeo), with Malvasía Riojana, Garnacha Blanca, Tempranillo Blanco (a natural mutation found in 1988 in Murillo de Río Leza), Maturana Blanca, Turruntés and, since 2008, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc and Verdejo. Recent changes also allow Albillo Mayor.
regions.styles: Reds dominate, in four ageing categories. Rioja's rules for reds are stricter than national law: a *crianza* spends two years ageing with at least one in 225-litre oak; a *reserva* three years with at least one in oak and six months in bottle; a *gran reserva* five years with at least two in oak and two in bottle. Whites and rosés have their own minimums (crianza 18 months with six in oak). Wines without an ageing claim are *Genérico*; since 2019 they may also use the softer term *madurado en bodega*. Classic whites from López de Heredia and Murrieta age in barrel for a decade; most modern whites are fresh Viura blends. Rosado is more and more often pale; the traditional, darker *clarete* is coming back. Quality sparkling wine has been allowed since 2017, with at least 15 months on lees and a 36-month *Gran Añada* category.
regions.classification: Rioja's hierarchy now runs in two directions at once. By ageing: Genérico, Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva. By place: Rioja; a zone (*Rioja Alta*, *Rioja Alavesa*, *Rioja Oriental*), which requires 100 percent of the grapes from that zone; a *vino de pueblo* (village wine, until 2022 called *vino de municipio*), at least 85 percent from one of 144 municipalities and made there; and *viñedo singular*, a single delimited vineyard at least 35 years old, owned or leased long-term, hand-harvested, with yields at least 20 percent below the DOCa limit (5,000 kg/ha for reds), and approved twice by tasting panels. The 2019 labelling rules added terms for old vines (35 years), centenarian vines (100 years), pre-phylloxera vines (before 1900), high-altitude vineyards (550 m), estate vineyards and estate bottling. Viñedos singulares were first recognised by ministerial order in 2019; by 2026 there were 167.

regions.name: Rioja Alta
regions.tagline: The cool western heart of classic Rioja, from Haro's station bodegas to the Najerilla valley.
regions.summary: Rioja Alta covers the western part of the DOCa, mostly on the south bank of the Ebro in La Rioja plus the Sonsierra on the north bank, and the small Burgos enclave of El Ternero. It holds Haro, Briones, Ollauri, Cenicero, Fuenmayor, San Asensio and Nájera, and most of the historic houses. Its wines are the most structured and slow-ageing in Rioja, the source of most great Gran Reservas.
regions.history: Haro's railway (1863) and the phylloxera boom made Rioja Alta the commercial centre of the region: the Barrio de la Estación holds a cluster of 19th-century bodegas unique in Spain. The monasteries of San Millán, in the Cárdenas valley, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site and the cradle of written Castilian.
regions.terroir: Altitudes of 450 to 700 m, an Atlantic-influenced climate with about 400 to 500 mm of rain, and ferrous clay, clay-limestone and alluvial terrace soils. Rivers from the Sierra de la Demanda (Oja, Tirón, Najerilla) cool the valleys.
regions.grapes: Tempranillo above all, with Graciano, Mazuelo, Garnacha in higher, poorer sites, and Viura and Malvasía for whites.
regions.styles: Classic oak-aged reds, the great Gran Reservas; long-aged whites at López de Heredia.
regions.classification: Zone wines labelled Rioja Alta must be 100% from the zone; many villages here have vino de pueblo status and dozens of viñedos singulares, especially in San Vicente de la Sonsierra, Briones and Haro.

regions.name: Rioja Alavesa
regions.tagline: Chalky terraces under the cliffs of the Sierra de Cantabria, in the Basque province of Álava.
regions.summary: Rioja Alavesa is the smallest zone, about 13,000 ha in 15 municipalities on the north bank of the Ebro, among them Laguardia, Elciego, Labastida, Samaniego, Lanciego, Oyón and Villabuena. It produces fine, aromatic Tempranillo, from carbonic-maceration cosechero wines to top single vineyards, and is home to Marqués de Riscal, Artadi, Remírez de Ganuza and Contino. Its growers have long pushed for their own identity: the attempt to create a separate DO, Arabako Mahastiak / Viñedos de Álava, was annulled by the Basque high court in November 2024.
regions.history: Laguardia, a walled medieval hill town, sits on top of hundreds of underground cellars. In 1858 Riscal built Spain's first modern bodega in Elciego. Alavesa families long made wine by carbonic maceration in stone *lagos*, sold young as *cosechero*.
regions.terroir: Limestone and clay-limestone soils on south-facing terraces between about 400 and 700 m, sheltered from northern weather by the Sierra de Cantabria and with the most Atlantic climate in Rioja.
regions.grapes: Tempranillo almost exclusively, with Viura and Malvasía.
regions.styles: Fresh carbonic young reds, elegant crianzas and reservas, and single-vineyard wines.
regions.classification: Álava holds 73 of Rioja's 167 viñedos singulares (2026). Zone wines must be 100% Alavesa grapes.

sources.title: El Derecho, TSJPV ruling on Viñedos de Álava

regions.name: Rioja Oriental
regions.tagline: The warm, Mediterranean east of Rioja, Garnacha's stronghold, renamed from Rioja Baja in 2018.
regions.summary: Rioja Oriental runs from Logroño's eastern edge to Alfaro along the lower Ebro and the valleys of the Leza, Cidacos and Alhama, including the Navarrese villages within the DOCa. Long dismissed as a source of blending wine, it is being reassessed: high Garnacha vineyards on Monte Yerga and around Tudelilla, Quel and Alfaro give some of Rioja's most exciting wines, notably Álvaro Palacios's Palacios Remondo and Quiñón de Valmira.
regions.history: The zone was called Rioja Baja (lower Rioja) until 2018, when the Consejo renamed it to avoid the implication of lower quality. The Palacios family has been based in Alfaro since 1945.
regions.terroir: Lower and warmer, mostly 300 to 500 m, with a Mediterranean climate, under 400 mm of rain and alluvial, clay and gravel soils; but slopes up to 700 m and more on Monte Yerga.
regions.grapes: Tempranillo is most planted, but Garnacha is the zone's signature.
regions.styles: Ripe reds, Garnacha, rosados.
regions.classification: Zone wines must be 100% Oriental grapes. Navarra's three viñedos singulares lie here.

regions.name: Castilla y León
regions.tagline: The high plateau of the Duero, where Tempranillo and Verdejo ripen under hot days and freezing nights.
regions.summary:
Spain's largest autonomous community holds its second great red-wine region and much else besides. The Duero flows west across the northern Meseta for some 400 km before it becomes Portugal's Douro, and along it lie Ribera del Duero, Rueda, Toro, Tierra del Vino de Zamora and Arribes; tributaries add Cigales (Pisuerga) and Arlanza. To the northwest, beyond the Montes de León, Bierzo belongs to the community but to Galicia's climate; León and the Valles de Benavente sit on the plains between. To the south, the Sierra de Gredos and the Sierra de Francia hold Cebreros and Sierra de Salamanca.

Castilla y León counted about 81,000 hectares of vineyard in 2025 and was one of the few regions still growing. It is also home to Vega Sicilia, Spain's most famous single estate, and to the region's oddest legal curiosity: some of its best-known wines (Mauro, Abadía Retuerta until 2022, and many others) are sold as Vino de la Tierra de Castilla y León because they lie just outside a DO, or prefer its freedom.
regions.history:
The vine came with the Romans and spread with the monasteries during the medieval repopulation of the Duero frontier: Cistercians at Valbuena (1143) and Premonstratensians at Retuerta (1146). Valladolid was a royal capital and its taverns drank the white wines of Rueda and La Seca, made oxidatively in underground cellars. The hillsides of Aranda de Duero, Roa, Peñafiel and Toro are pierced by underground cellars from the 13th to 18th centuries, dug to keep wine cool through hot summers; Aranda alone has kilometres of galleries under its old town.

Phylloxera, emigration and cooperative bulk wine left the region quiet until 1982, when Ribera del Duero won its DO thanks to a handful of growers led by Alejandro Fernández of Pesquera. Robert Parker's praise in the late 1980s, and the long shadow of Vega Sicilia, made it famous almost overnight. Rueda (1980) reinvented itself with fresh Verdejo after Marqués de Riscal arrived in 1972, and Toro (1987) followed with powerful reds that attracted Vega Sicilia, the Lurtons, Numanthia and Bordeaux investors in the late 1990s.
regions.terroir: This is a high continental plateau: 700 to 1,000 m, with less than 450 mm of rain, hot dry summers, very cold winters, spring frosts and a short growing season. The swing between day and night in late summer can exceed 20 degrees, which preserves acidity and colour in Tempranillo. Soils vary from limestone and marl on the slopes of Ribera to sandy, gravelly, pebbly terraces in Rueda and Toro, where sand also protected some vines from phylloxera. Rivers temper frost on the valley floors, while the best sites sit on mid-slope *cuestas* and *páramos* (high limestone tablelands).
regions.grapes: Tempranillo, called Tinto Fino or Tinta del País in Ribera and Tinta de Toro in Toro; Verdejo in Rueda; Garnacha in Cigales, Gredos and Toro; Mencía and Godello in Bierzo; Prieto Picudo in León; Juan García in Arribes; Rufete in Sierra de Salamanca; Albillo Mayor for Ribera's whites.
regions.styles: Powerful oak-aged reds (Ribera, Toro), fresh and lees-aged whites (Rueda), traditional pale claretes (Cigales), mountain reds (Bierzo, Gredos, Arribes).
regions.classification: Nine DOs, four Vinos de Calidad (Valles de Benavente, Valtiendas, Sierra de Salamanca, Cebreros) and three Vinos de Pago (Abadía Retuerta, Dehesa Peñalba and Urueña), plus the large IGP Vino de la Tierra de Castilla y León used by many estates outside the DOs.

sources.title: Wein.plus, Spain's vineyard area 2025 by region

regions.name: Galicia
regions.tagline: Atlantic Spain: granite, rain, Albariño on stone pergolas and Mencía on the river terraces of the Sil.
regions.summary:
Galicia, in Spain's green northwest corner, is a country of its own for wine: Atlantic, granitic, wet, with its own language and a deep attachment to native grapes. Its five DOs are Rías Baixas on the coast, Ribeiro in the Avia and Miño valleys, Ribeira Sacra in the canyons of the Sil and Miño, Valdeorras further up the Sil, and Monterrei on the Portuguese border. Vineyards are tiny, fragmented into minifundios, and often trained high on granite posts (*parras*) to keep grapes away from damp ground.

For most of the 20th century Galicia made rustic local wine from hybrid and high-yielding vines. The modern story starts with the rescue of native grapes in the 1970s and 1980s: Albariño in the Salnés, Godello in Valdeorras, Treixadura in Ribeiro, Mencía and Merenzao on the Sil. Today Rías Baixas is one of Spain's most valuable white-wine regions and Ribeira Sacra one of its most exciting red ones.
regions.history: The Romans dug terraces in the Sil canyon and Benedictine and Cistercian monasteries, Santo Estevo, San Clodio, Oseira, Montederramo, spread viticulture through the Middle Ages. Ribeiro's wines were exported to England and Flanders in the 14th to 16th centuries from Ribadavia. Phylloxera and oidium in the 19th century, then mass emigration, emptied the vineyards. Revival came with Rías Baixas's DO (1988) and the recovery of native varieties.
regions.terroir: Atlantic climate: 1,000 to 1,800 mm of rain on the coast, mild temperatures, high humidity, with more continental warmth inland along the Miño and Sil. Granite dominates on the coast and in Ribeiro; slate and schist in Ribeira Sacra, Valdeorras and Monterrei.
regions.grapes: Albariño, Treixadura, Loureiro, Godello, Caíño Blanco, Torrontés, Lado, Dona Branca; reds Mencía, Merenzao (Bastardo/Trousseau), Sousón, Caíño Tinto, Brancellao, Espadeiro, Garnacha Tintorera.
regions.styles: Fresh aromatic whites; light and mineral reds from the river canyons; rare tostado sweet wines in Ribeiro and Valdeorras.
regions.classification: Five DOs plus the IGPs Barbanza e Iria, Betanzos and Val do Miño-Ourense. Rías Baixas and Ribeira Sacra have subzones.

regions.name: Bierzo
regions.tagline: A mountain bowl in León that behaves like Galicia: Mencía on slate, and Spain's most Burgundian classification.
regions.summary: Bierzo is a basin ringed by mountains in the northwest of León province, on the Camino de Santiago, with a climate halfway between Galicia's Atlantic and Castile's continental. Its 2,300 hectares of vineyard are dominated by old Mencía on slate and clay, and its 2019 classification of villages and parajes is the most Burgundy-like in Spain.
regions.history: Roman miners at Las Médulas, medieval monasteries on the pilgrim road (over two dozen in the comarca before the 1830s confiscations), and later cooperatives shaped the region. Álvaro Palacios and his nephew Ricardo Pérez arrived in 1999 and Raúl Pérez, a native of Valtuille, became Spain's most influential winemaker of his generation.
regions.terroir: A sheltered depression at 450 to 900 m. The valley floor has deep clay and alluvial soils; the best wines come from the slopes of slate and quartzite around Corullón, Valtuille and the Ancares hills.
regions.grapes: Mencía (about 70% of grapes), Garnacha Tintorera, Merenzao, Estaladiña; whites Godello, Doña Blanca, Palomino.
regions.styles: Fresh to structured Mencía reds, Godello whites, rosados.
regions.classification: Since 2019: Vino de Región (Bierzo), Vino de Villa, Vino de Paraje, Vino de Viña Clasificada and Gran Vino de Viña Clasificada.

regions.name: Basque Country
regions.tagline: Txakoli: spritzy, salty whites from the green hills above the Bay of Biscay.
regions.summary: The Basque Country holds two different wine worlds: Rioja Alavesa in the south (part of DOCa Rioja) and three small DOs for Txakoli, the fresh, low-alcohol, slightly spritzy white wine of the Atlantic coast, traditionally poured from a height into a tumbler in the pintxo bars of San Sebastián and Bilbao.
regions.history: Txakoli was a household wine of Basque farms (*baserriak*) for centuries and nearly disappeared in the 20th century. The DOs Getariako Txakolina (1989), Bizkaiko Txakolina (1994) and Arabako Txakolina (2001) revived it.
regions.terroir: Cool, very wet Atlantic hills (1,200 to 1,600 mm of rain), with vines on high trellises and pergolas on clay and sandstone slopes near the sea.
regions.grapes: Hondarrabi Zuri (white), Hondarrabi Beltza (red), Gros and Petit Manseng, Izkiriota.
regions.styles: Fresh, spritzy whites; rosé (rosado or *ojo de gallo*); a little red.
regions.classification: Three Txakoli DOs.
appellations: Getariako Txakolina / Chacolí de Getaria / Txakolí de Getaria
Bizkaiko Txakolina / Chacolí de Bizkaia / Txakolí de Bizkaia
Arabako Txakolina / Txakolí de Álava / Chacolí de Álava

regions.name: Asturias
regions.tagline: Steep mountain vineyards of Cangas del Narcea, kept alive by a handful of growers.
regions.summary: Asturias is cider country, but in the southwest, around Cangas del Narcea, monks and peasants grew vines on steep slate slopes for centuries. The Vino de Calidad Cangas protects them.
regions.history: The monastery of Corias, founded in the 11th century, is credited with spreading the vine here.
regions.terroir: Steep slate and quartzite slopes at 400 to 900 m above the Narcea, cool and wet.
regions.grapes: Albarín Negro, Carrasquín, Verdejo Negro, Mencía; Albarín Blanco.
regions.styles: Light, fresh reds and whites.
regions.classification: VC Cangas.

regions.name: Navarra
regions.tagline: From Pyrenean foothills to the Ebro's semi-desert: rosado heritage, Garnacha and four single-estate pagos.
regions.summary: Navarra's wine country runs from cool valleys near Pamplona to the hot, dry Ribera along the Ebro. The DO Navarra (about 8,800 ha) made its name with Garnacha rosado, then reinvented itself in the 1980s with Tempranillo and French varieties; today old Garnacha is back in fashion. The southwest corner of Navarra also belongs to DOCa Rioja, and the community has four Vinos de Pago: Arínzano, Otazu, Prado de Irache and Bolandín.
regions.history: Navarra was an independent kingdom until 1512, and its monasteries on the Camino de Santiago, Irache, Leyre and La Oliva, kept vineyards. EVENA, the regional viticulture research station founded in Olite in 1981, led the switch to international varieties. Chivite, founded in 1647, is one of Spain's oldest wine families.
regions.terroir: Five subzones: Baja Montaña (cool, northeast, Garnacha), Valdizarbe (around Puente la Reina), Tierra Estella (west, cooler), Ribera Alta (centre, around Olite and Tafalla) and Ribera Baja (the hot, dry south around Tudela). Soils are limestone and clay, gravel and alluvium.
regions.grapes: Garnacha, Tempranillo, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Graciano; Chardonnay, Viura, Moscatel de Grano Menudo.
regions.styles: Rosado, Garnacha and Tempranillo reds, Bordeaux blends, sweet Moscatel.
regions.classification: DO Navarra with five subzones; four Vinos de Pago.

regions.name: Aragón
regions.tagline: Garnacha's homeland: old bush vines on the slopes of the Moncayo and the Sierra de Algairén, and the cool Somontano below the Pyrenees.
regions.summary: Aragón is where Garnacha (and probably Cariñena, named after the town) came from. Its four DOs, Campo de Borja, Calatayud and Cariñena in the province of Zaragoza and Somontano in Huesca, plus two pagos (Aylés and Urbezo), make wine from very old Garnacha vineyards at high altitude, much of it exported at great value.
regions.history: The Cistercians of Veruela (1146) planted Campo de Borja. Cariñena's DO dates from 1932, one of Spain's first. In the 1990s and 2000s exporters and Americans like Jorge Ordóñez and Eric Solomon championed old-vine Aragonese Garnacha.
regions.terroir: Continental, dry, with the cold northwest wind called the *cierzo*. Soils are slate and quartzite in Calatayud, limestone and clay in Borja, slate and gravel in Cariñena; Somontano is cooler at the Pyrenees' foot.
regions.grapes: Garnacha, Cariñena (Mazuela), Tempranillo, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot; Macabeo, Garnacha Blanca, Chardonnay, Gewürztraminer.
regions.styles: Garnacha reds, rosados, international blends in Somontano.
regions.classification: Four DOs and two Vinos de Pago.

sources.title: MAPA, Urbezo vino de pago registered (2024)

regions.name: Catalonia
regions.tagline: Cava's homeland and Priorat's black slate: a Mediterranean region of cooperatives, monasteries and restless growers.
regions.summary:
Catalonia has eleven wine DOs, from the giant regional DO Catalunya to tiny Alella, plus most of the vineyards of DO Cava. It is Spain's sparkling-wine capital (Sant Sadurní d'Anoia alone holds dozens of cellars), and its interior hides some of Europe's most dramatic red-wine vineyards in Priorat and Montsant. It is also the most argumentative wine region in Spain: since 2012 a string of leading sparkling producers have left Cava for their own labels, and Penedès became, from the 2025 harvest, the first fully organic DO in the world.

The modernisme movement left a remarkable legacy here: the early 20th-century cooperative wineries of Falset, Gandesa, Pinell de Brai, L'Espluga de Francolí and others, designed by Cèsar Martinell and Pere Domènech i Roura, are known as the *catedrals del vi*, cathedrals of wine.
regions.history: The Romans grew wine on the Laietanian coast (Alella, the Maresme) and around Tarraco, and shipped it across the empire. Medieval monasteries, Scala Dei (1194), Poblet (1151), Santes Creus and Sant Pere de Rodes, kept the vine. In the 18th and 19th centuries Reus became a hub for brandy and wine, and Catalonia boomed when phylloxera struck France, until it arrived in the Empordà in 1879 and destroyed most vineyards by the 1890s. The response was the cooperative movement, and, in Penedès, the replanting of white grapes for sparkling wine after Josep Raventós made the first bottles at Codorníu in 1872.
regions.terroir: Mostly Mediterranean, from humid coast to dry interior plateaus. Soils include the granitic *sauló* of Alella, the limestone and clay of Penedès, the slate *llicorella* of Priorat, the chalky soils of Terra Alta and Conca de Barberà, and the gravel and limestone of Costers del Segre. The tramuntana wind sweeps the Empordà, the garbinada sea breeze cools Terra Alta.
regions.grapes: Xarel·lo, Macabeu, Parellada (Cava trio), Garnatxa Blanca, Picapoll, Pansa Blanca; reds Garnatxa, Samsó (Cariñena), Ull de Llebre (Tempranillo), Trepat, Sumoll, Monastrell, plus international varieties.
regions.styles: Traditional-method sparkling, structured old-vine reds, Mediterranean whites, rancio and sweet Garnatxa.
regions.classification: One DOQ (Priorat), ten DOs, Cava (supra-autonomic). Priorat has the vi de vila and paratge system; Cava has zones and Paraje Calificado; Penedès has Clàssic Penedès; Corpinnat is a private collective brand outside the DO system.

regions.name: Priorat
regions.tagline: Black slate, Carthusian history and the 1989 revolution that put Spain on the fine-wine map.
regions.summary:
Priorat is a small, wild, mountainous region in the hills of Tarragona, ringed by the cliffs of the Montsant range. Its vines grow on *llicorella*, a crumbling slate and quartzite that makes up about 90 percent of the subsoil, on terraces and slopes so steep that mules are still used. The yields are tiny and the wines are dense, mineral and long-lived.

For centuries the region was governed by the Carthusians of Scala Dei, founded in 1194 by monks from Provence; *priorat* means the domain of a prior. After phylloxera hit in the 1890s, the vineyards were abandoned and the people left. In 1989 five friends, René Barbier, Álvaro Palacios, Daphne Glorian, Josep Lluís Pérez and Carles Pastrana, pooled their first harvest in Gratallops, making the wines that became Clos Mogador, L'Ermita, Clos Erasmus, Clos Martinet and Clos de l'Obac. In a decade the 'Gang of Five' made Priorat one of the world's most famous regions. The DOQ (DOCa) came in 2000, nationally confirmed in 2009.
regions.history: Scala Dei was founded in 1194; its lands, the historic Priorat, stayed under monastic rule until the 1835 confiscations. Phylloxera arrived at the end of the 19th century. The 1989 revival led to the DOQ in 2000. In 2007 the vi de vila system began, and in 2017 vi de paratge and classified vineyards; the January 2024 register lists L'Ermita, Mas de la Rosa and Tossal d'en Bou as Gran Vinya Classificada.
regions.terroir: Steep slate (llicorella) slopes and terraces at 100 to 750 m, a Mediterranean-continental climate with 400 to 600 mm of rain, hot dry summers and cool nights. The Montsant cliffs block northern winds; the Siurana river drains the basin.
regions.grapes: Garnatxa and Samsó (Cariñena), the old-vine pillars, with Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah and Merlot; whites Garnatxa Blanca, Macabeu, Pedro Ximénez.
regions.styles: Concentrated, mineral reds; a small amount of white; historic rancio and sweet wines.
regions.classification: The pyramid *Els noms de la terra*: DOQ Priorat, Vi de Vila (12 zones: Bellmunt del Priorat, Gratallops, el Lloar, la Morera de Montsant, Porrera, Poboleda, Scala Dei, Torroja del Priorat, la Vilella Alta, la Vilella Baixa, Masos de Falset and Solanes del Molar), Vi de Paratge (459 named sites), Vinya Classificada and Gran Vinya Classificada (at least 80% of vines 35 years old, yields of 3,000 kg/ha for reds, at least 90% Garnatxa and Samsó). Vineyards over 75 years old or planted before 1945 carry a special Vinyes Velles protection.

sources.title: DOQ Priorat, Els noms de la terra leaflet (2019)
Spanish Wine Lover, guide to Priorat's classification

regions.name: Penedès
regions.tagline: The heart of Spanish sparkling wine, now the world's first all-organic DO.
regions.summary: Penedès, between Barcelona and Tarragona, holds about 26,000 hectares of vines, most of them supplying Cava. Its own DO (just over 13,000 registered hectares) became 100% organic from the 2025 harvest. Sant Sadurní d'Anoia is the capital of Cava; Vilafranca del Penedès of still wine. Since the 2010s the DO's own Clàssic Penedès category and the Corpinnat brand have offered alternatives to Cava for the region's finest sparkling wines.
regions.history: Roman villas and amphora kilns dot the region. Josep Raventós made Spain's first traditional-method sparkling wine at Codorníu in 1872, and after phylloxera white grapes replaced reds. Torres, Jean Leon and Can Ràfols dels Caus brought international varieties from the 1960s; Albet i Noya pioneered organics in 1978.
regions.terroir: Three tiers from coast to mountains: the warm Baix Penedès, the central Medio Penedès plain, and the higher Alt Penedès toward Montserrat, up to about 800 m. Limestone and clay soils dominate, with the Garraf massif on the coast.
regions.grapes: Xarel·lo (the signature), Macabeu, Parellada; Garnatxa, Ull de Llebre, Cabernet, Merlot, Sumoll.
regions.styles: Sparkling (Cava, Clàssic Penedès, Corpinnat), still whites and reds.
regions.classification: DO Penedès (all organic since 2025) with Clàssic Penedès for sparkling; DO Cava overlaps it; Corpinnat is a private brand.

sources.title: Foods & Wines from Spain, Penedès 100% organic harvest (Dec 2025)

regions.name: Castilla-La Mancha
regions.tagline: Don Quixote's plain: almost half of Spain's vines, Airén and Tempranillo, and more Vinos de Pago than anywhere else.
regions.summary:
Castilla-La Mancha grows about 422,000 hectares of vines, 47.5 percent of Spain's wine-grape vineyard in 2025, which also makes it the largest single wine region on earth. Most of it lies on the high plain of La Mancha, at 600 to 800 m, a land of windmills, red clay, limestone and extreme continental weather where vines were traditionally planted wide apart as low bush vines to survive drought.

For most of the 20th century La Mancha supplied bulk wine and brandy base, much of it from Airén, a white grape that once covered more land than any other variety on earth. Since the 1990s the region has switched heavily to Tempranillo (locally Cencibel) and international varieties, with irrigation and trellising. Its quality frontier is in the higher, fringe areas: the Montes de Toledo, Manchuela's Bobal, Méntrida's Garnacha, Uclés, and an archipelago of single-estate Vinos de Pago, 14 of Spain's 28 in 2026.
regions.history: Cervantes's Don Quixote (1605) is full of La Mancha's wine, from Sancho's wineskins to the earthenware *tinajas* of El Toboso. The railway to Madrid in the 1860s turned Valdepeñas into the capital's tavern supplier. Phylloxera reached here late, and cooperatives dominated after the 1950s. Carlos Falcó's Dominio de Valdepusa became Spain's first Vino de Pago in 2003.
regions.terroir: High plateau with hot, dry summers (often over 40 degrees), cold winters, 300 to 400 mm of rain; red clay and sandy soils over limestone. Fringe areas rise to 1,000 m in Albacete and the Montes de Toledo. Campo de Calatrava has volcanic soils.
regions.grapes: Airén, Tempranillo (Cencibel), Garnacha, Bobal, Monastrell, Garnacha Tintorera, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Petit Verdot, Merlot; Macabeo, Verdejo, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Moscatel.
regions.styles: Bulk and value reds and whites, oak-aged Tempranillo, single-estate reds.
regions.classification: Nine DOs (La Mancha, Valdepeñas, Manchuela, Méntrida, Mondéjar, Ribera del Júcar, Uclés, Almansa, Campo de Calatrava), part of Jumilla, and 14 Vinos de Pago. The IGP Vino de la Tierra de Castilla is widely used.

regions.name: Madrid
regions.tagline: The capital's own wine, and the Garnacha revival of the Sierra de Gredos.
regions.summary: The DO Vinos de Madrid has four subzones around the capital. For centuries they supplied Madrid's taverns; today the action is in the west, in San Martín de Valdeiglesias, where old Garnacha on granite in the foothills of the Sierra de Gredos makes some of Spain's most sought-after reds.
regions.history: Madrid's vineyards were the capital's wine supply until the railway brought cheaper La Mancha wine. The Gredos revival began in the 2000s with Bernabeleva, Marañones and Comando G.
regions.terroir: Granite and sandy soils in the west (San Martín, up to 900 m), clay and limestone in Arganda, sand and clay in Navalcarnero.
regions.grapes: Garnacha, Tempranillo, Malvar (local white), Albillo Real, Airén.
regions.styles: Fresh mountain Garnacha, Albillo whites, everyday reds.
regions.classification: DO Vinos de Madrid with four subzones: Arganda, Navalcarnero, San Martín de Valdeiglesias and El Molar.

regions.name: Valencia
regions.tagline: Bobal on the Requena plateau, Moscatel by the sea and the centuries-old Fondillón of Alicante.
regions.summary: The Valencian Community has three DOs, Valencia, Utiel-Requena and Alicante, plus five Vinos de Pago, all on the Requena-Utiel plateau. It is a region of contrasts: the high, cold plateau of Utiel-Requena (700 to 900 m), where Bobal makes dark reds and Cava is made too; and the warm coast, where Moscatel de Alejandría grows for sweet wines and Monastrell gives Alicante its rich reds and the historic Fondillón.
regions.history: Iberian winemakers at Alt de Benimaquia near Dénia in the 6th century BC; Valencia's port shipped wine across the Mediterranean and, in the 19th century, to France during phylloxera. Requena's underground *cuevas* stored wine under the medieval town.
regions.terroir: From limestone and clay plateaus to coastal hills; Mediterranean climate inland becoming continental at altitude.
regions.grapes: Bobal, Monastrell, Tempranillo, Garnacha Tintorera, Garnacha; Moscatel de Alejandría, Merseguera, Macabeo, Malvasía.
regions.styles: Bobal reds and rosados, Monastrell reds, sweet Moscatel, Fondillón.
regions.classification: DO Valencia (four subzones), DO Utiel-Requena, DO Alicante (two subzones), Vinos de Pago El Terrerazo, Los Balagueses, Chozas Carrascal, Vera de Estenas and Tharsys.

sources.title: Wine, Wit and Wisdom, Vino de Pago Tharsys (2025)

regions.name: Murcia
regions.tagline: Monastrell country: ungrafted bush vines in the near-desert of Jumilla, Yecla and Bullas.
regions.summary: Murcia's three DOs, Jumilla (shared with Albacete), Yecla and Bullas, are the world's great homeland of Monastrell (Mourvèdre). In a semi-arid landscape with under 300 mm of rain, old bush vines on chalky and sandy soils give dark, sun-baked but increasingly fresh reds.
regions.history: Jumilla's sandy soils kept phylloxera away until 1989, when the louse finally arrived and destroyed much of its ungrafted vineyard, prompting replanting and modernisation.
regions.terroir: High plateaus at 400 to 900 m, continental and dry, with limestone, chalk and sandy soils.
regions.grapes: Monastrell, Garnacha Tintorera, Syrah, Tempranillo, Cabernet; Airén, Macabeo, Merseguera, Moscatel.
regions.styles: Rich Monastrell reds, rosados, sweet Monastrell.
regions.classification: Three DOs; Jumilla crosses into Albacete.

regions.name: Extremadura
regions.tagline: Tierra de Barros and the Guadiana: one of Spain's largest vineyards, still little known.
regions.summary: Extremadura, on the Portuguese border, had about 76,500 hectares of vines in 2025, most of it around Almendralejo in the Tierra de Barros, a plain of rich clay. Its single DO, Ribera del Guadiana, has six subzones. Almendralejo is also a Cava zone and the home of a large sparkling-wine industry.
regions.history: The Romans founded Emerita Augusta (Mérida) here; wine has been made since. Almendralejo grew as a wine town in the 19th century, and its Cava production dates from the 1980s.
regions.terroir: Hot plains of clay (*barros*) and sand, with continental extremes and little rain.
regions.grapes: Tempranillo, Garnacha, Cabernet, Syrah; Pardina, Cayetana Blanca, Macabeo, Eva (Beba).
regions.styles: Value reds and whites, Cava.
regions.classification: DO Ribera del Guadiana with subzones; part of DO Cava (Viñedos de Almendralejo zone).

regions.name: Andalusia
regions.tagline: Spain's ancient south: flor, solera, raisined Pedro Ximénez and mountain Moscatel.
regions.summary:
Andalusia is the cradle of Spanish wine and the home of its most original styles. Phoenicians planted vines near Cádiz three thousand years ago, and from the late Middle Ages to the 20th century the region's wines, Sherry, Málaga and Montilla, were among the most traded in the world. Today Andalusia's vineyard is smaller than it was, and still white wines and reds are a growing minority, but the region's fortified and oxidative wines, aged in soleras for years or decades, remain some of the greatest values and most profound wines on earth.

The region's DOs are Jerez-Xérès-Sherry and Manzanilla-Sanlúcar de Barrameda (which share one vineyard and one Consejo Regulador), Montilla-Moriles in Córdoba, Málaga and Sierras de Málaga (also sharing a Consejo), Condado de Huelva, Granada, and the Vino de Calidad Lebrija.
regions.history: Phoenician Gadir (Cádiz) and the winepress at Doña Blanca; Roman Baetica's olive oil and wine trade; Moorish Sherish; the English sack trade after the 1400s; Drake's 1587 raid; the 18th and 19th century boom of British, Irish and French-founded Sherry houses; phylloxera, which entered Spain at Málaga in 1878; and the Sherry crisis of the late 20th century, when sales collapsed and vineyards were grubbed up.
regions.terroir: From the Atlantic-cooled albariza hills of Jerez to the hot Campiña of Córdoba and the steep slate mountains of the Axarquía and Ronda. Summers are very hot and dry; winters mild and wet.
regions.grapes: Palomino Fino, Pedro Ximénez, Moscatel de Alejandría, Moscatel Morisco, Zalema, Listán de Huelva, Vijiriega; reds Tempranillo, Syrah, Garnacha, Romé, Tintilla de Rota.
regions.styles: Biologically aged (fino, manzanilla), oxidative (oloroso), hybrid (amontillado, palo cortado), naturally sweet (PX, Moscatel), plus new still whites and reds.
regions.classification: Six DOs and one VC. Sherry has its own systems: solera and criaderas, VOS (over 20 years) and VORS (over 30) certification, age statements of 12 and 15 years, and since 2021 pago names and unfortified wines.

regions.name: Sherry Country
regions.tagline: The Marco de Jerez: white albariza hills, Atlantic winds and the slow alchemy of flor and solera.
regions.summary:
The Marco de Jerez is the land between the Guadalquivir and the Guadalete in the province of Cádiz, with Jerez de la Frontera, Sanlúcar de Barrameda and El Puerto de Santa María at its corners, the famous Sherry Triangle. Ten municipalities make up the production zone: Jerez, El Puerto, Sanlúcar, Trebujena, Chipiona, Rota, Puerto Real, Chiclana, San José del Valle, and Lebrija in Seville province. Around 7,000 hectares of vineyard (7,027 ha in 2022) are farmed by about 1,500 growers.

Sherry is not one wine but a family. All start as dry white wine from Palomino. Wines destined for *biological ageing* are fortified to about 15 percent and kept in barrels (butts, *botas*, of about 600 litres, filled only five-sixths) under a living film of yeast called *flor*, which protects them from oxygen and feeds on alcohol, glycerine and acidity, leaving a pale, bone-dry, tangy wine smelling of bread dough and almonds: *fino* in Jerez and El Puerto, *manzanilla* in Sanlúcar. Wines destined for *oxidative ageing* are fortified to 17 percent or more, which kills flor, and age in contact with air, growing darker, nuttier and more concentrated: *oloroso*. In between, *amontillado* starts as a fino and continues as an oloroso when the flor dies, and *palo cortado*, rare and prized, combines an amontillado's finesse with an oloroso's body. *Pedro Ximénez* and *Moscatel* are made from sun-dried grapes, the sweetest wines in the world.

All of these age in a *solera*: rows of barrels arranged in scales (*criaderas*). A portion of wine, the *saca*, is drawn from the oldest scale (the solera) for bottling, and that barrel is refilled (*rocío*) from the next oldest criadera, and so on up the scales. The result is a wine with no vintage, an average age that can reach decades, and a consistent house character kept alive across centuries.
regions.history:
Phoenicians at Gadir and Doña Blanca, Roman Ceret (Xera), and Moorish Sherish all made wine here. After Alfonso X took Jerez in 1264, the vineyards expanded, and by the 15th century wine was shipped from Sanlúcar to England and Flanders. In 1587 Francis Drake's raid on Cádiz carried off some 2,900 butts, and the English fashion for 'sherris-sack', immortalised by Shakespeare's Falstaff, began.

The great houses rose in the 18th and 19th centuries, many founded by British, Irish and French families: Garvey (1780), Osborne (1772), Sandeman (1790), Domecq, González Byass (1835), Williams & Humbert (1877), Harveys of Bristol. The solera system probably developed in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, when shippers needed consistent wines. Jerez was among the first Spanish DOs, with its Consejo Regulador formed in 1935. Sherry boomed through the 1970s, then sales collapsed: from more than 150 million bottles a year to a fraction of that today, and the vineyard shrank from more than 20,000 hectares to about 7,000.

The modern renaissance began in the 2000s with *en rama* bottlings, Equipo Navazos's *La Bota* series (from 2005), single-cask releases from *almacenistas* (stockholders who aged wine for the big houses), and a generation of growers, Ramiro Ibáñez, Willy Pérez and others, arguing for vineyard and vintage. In September 2021 the Consejo approved the deepest reform in its history: ageing allowed anywhere in the production zone (in force from October 2022), pago names on labels, recovery of historic varieties, unfortified wines, and new categories for very old biological wines.
regions.terroir:
The heart of Sherry is *albariza*, a brilliant white soil of chalk, clay and silica formed from the shells of diatoms and radiolaria in an ancient sea. It soaks up winter rain like a sponge, then forms a hard crust in summer that keeps moisture in, letting dry-farmed vines survive five months without rain; its whiteness reflects light into the canopy. The best albariza lies on gentle hills (*lomas*) and is divided into historic *pagos*, named vineyard districts: Macharnudo, Carrascal, Balbaína, Añina, Los Tercios, Miraflores, Maína and others. Darker clay soils (*barros*) and sands (*arenas*) gave Moscatel and lesser Palomino.

The climate is shaped by two winds. The *poniente* blows in from the Atlantic, humid and cool, bringing night dew to the vineyards and moisture to the bodegas, which flor needs. The *levante*, a hot, dry wind from the east, can blow for days, drying grapes and stressing vines, and thinning the flor. Sanlúcar, at the mouth of the Guadalquivir across from the marshes of Doñana, gets the most humidity, so its flor is thickest and lasts all year, which gives manzanilla its lighter, saltier, more delicate character. Bodegas, the 'cathedrals' of Jerez, have high ceilings, thick walls and windows facing the poniente, built to stay cool and humid.
regions.grapes: Palomino Fino (over 95%), Pedro Ximénez, Moscatel de Alejandría; since 2021 historic varieties such as Beba, Perruno, Vigiriega, Mantúo de Pilas and Mantúo Castellano are allowed again (Manzanilla remains Palomino-only).
regions.styles: Manzanilla and Manzanilla Pasada; Fino and Fino Viejo; Amontillado; Palo Cortado; Oloroso; Pedro Ximénez; Moscatel; Dulce; and blended Pale Cream, Medium and Cream. Since the reform, also unfortified wines (at least 15% natural alcohol and two years' ageing) and pago-labelled wines.
regions.classification:
Age matters more than origin. Every Sherry must have an average age of at least two years. Two age-certified categories, tested by carbon dating and tasting, cover very old amontillado, oloroso, palo cortado and PX: *VOS* (*Vinum Optimum Signatum*, Very Old Sherry, over 20 years) and *VORS* (*Vinum Optimum Rare Signatum*, Very Old Rare Sherry, over 30 years); there are also certified 12-year and 15-year age statements. *Manzanilla Pasada* and *Fino Viejo* (formerly Fino Antiguo) designate biological wines with at least seven years. *En rama* indicates minimal filtration, a style made famous from 2010 by Tío Pepe En Rama.

Since the 2021 reform, the Consejo certifies about 120 delimited pagos, and a label can name one if at least 85 percent of the grapes come from it. *Jerez Superior*, the historic name for the albariza heartland, is being revived as a category for top vineyards. An update reported in August 2026 also lowers the minimum strength of fino and pale cream from 15 to 14 percent. Wines labelled Manzanilla must be aged in Sanlúcar; wines aged in Sanlúcar may also be sold as Jerez.

regions.name: Canary Islands
regions.tagline: Volcanic islands with ungrafted pre-phylloxera vines, braided trunks and the ghost of Shakespeare's Canary sack.
regions.summary:
The Canary Islands, off the coast of Morocco, are one of the strangest and most exciting wine regions in the world. Phylloxera never reached them, so most vines grow on their own roots, some of them very old, and the islands keep dozens of varieties that disappeared elsewhere. Their soils are volcanic: black ash (*picón*), lava and red clay. Their climate is subtropical but tempered by the cool Canary Current and the trade winds (*alisios*), which bring clouds and moisture to the north faces of the islands.

The archipelago has eleven wine DOs: Lanzarote, La Palma, El Hierro, La Gomera and Gran Canaria (one per island), five on Tenerife (Tacoronte-Acentejo, Valle de la Orotava, Ycoden-Daute-Isora, Valle de Güímar and Abona), and the regional Islas Canarias, created in 2011, which lets producers blend across islands. Together they had about 6,300 registered hectares in 2023/24. Since the 2010s, producers like Suertes del Marqués, Envínate, Borja Pérez and Victoria Torres have made the Canaries a cult name.
regions.history: Castilian conquest (1402 to 1496) brought vines from Andalusia and Madeira. In the 16th and 17th centuries sweet Malvasía, 'Canary sack', was a luxury in England: Shakespeare's Sir Toby Belch calls for 'a cup of canary' in Twelfth Night, and the trade made fortunes in the ports of Garachico and Puerto de la Cruz. An English attempt to monopolise the trade through a chartered Canary Company in the 1660s provoked riots and boycotts, and in 1706 an eruption buried Garachico's harbour. Madeira and Port took Canary's place. Lanzarote's La Geria landscape was born after the Timanfaya eruptions of 1730 to 1736 buried the island's fields under ash.
regions.terroir: Volcanic soils from fresh ash to old weathered clays; altitudes from sea level to about 1,700 m in Tenerife's Abona; a mild climate with trade-wind clouds on the north slopes and dry, sunny south slopes.
regions.grapes: Listán Negro, Listán Blanco (Palomino), Malvasía Volcánica, Malvasía Aromática, Negramoll (Tinta Negra), Vijariego Blanco and Negro, Baboso Negro, Tintilla, Marmajuelo, Gual (Boal), Albillo Criollo, Forastera.
regions.styles: Fresh volcanic whites and reds, traditional maceración carbónica reds, sweet Malvasía.
regions.classification: Eleven DOs (Islas Canarias is formally a Vino de Calidad in the ministry list).

regions.name: Balearic Islands
regions.tagline: Mallorca's native Manto Negro and Callet, from the Tramuntana foothills to the island's east.
regions.summary: Mallorca has two DOs, Binissalem in the centre and Pla i Llevant in the east, plus several IGPs (Vi de la Terra Mallorca, Serra de Tramuntana, Illes Balears, Ibiza, Menorca, Formentera). Native grapes Manto Negro, Callet, Gorgollassa and Prensal Blanc give a Mediterranean island accent.
regions.history: Romans grew vines on Mallorca, and by the 19th century the island exported wine to France during phylloxera, before phylloxera struck here in 1891. Revival began in the 1990s.
regions.terroir: Mediterranean, warm and dry; Binissalem is sheltered by the Serra de Tramuntana, with calcareous soils and red clays (*call vermell*).
regions.grapes: Manto Negro, Callet, Gorgollassa, Fogoneu, Cabernet, Syrah; Prensal Blanc (Moll), Giró Ros, Chardonnay.
regions.styles: Reds and whites with Mediterranean warmth.
regions.classification: Two DOs, with IGPs for the rest.

appellations.name: Rioja
appellations.grapes: Tempranillo (about 88% of reds), Garnacha, Mazuelo, Graciano, Maturana Tinta; whites Viura, Malvasía Riojana, Garnacha Blanca, Tempranillo Blanco, Maturana Blanca, Turruntés, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Verdejo
appellations.summary:
Rioja is the benchmark Spanish red and, with 66,500 registered hectares and around 2.4 million hectolitres sold a year, also one of Europe's largest fine-wine regions. The classic Rioja is a blend led by Tempranillo, aged in 225-litre barrels, traditionally American oak, until it turns soft and savoury: strawberry and dried cherry, vanilla and dill, leather and tobacco. That style was learned from Bordeaux in the 1850s to 1880s and is still made beautifully by López de Heredia, La Rioja Alta, CVNE and Muga, whose Gran Reservas can live for half a century.

From the 1990s, a modern wave led by Artadi, Roda, Remírez de Ganuza, Finca Allende and Benjamín Romeo made darker, riper wines in new French oak, sold on the name of a vineyard rather than an ageing category. Today the most interesting movement is about place: Telmo Rodríguez and Remelluri, Sierra Cantabria, Olivier Rivière, Abel Mendoza and many small growers in San Vicente de la Sonsierra and Rioja Alavesa make transparent wines from old field blends, often from bush vines high on the slopes. The rules have followed: since 2017 a label can name one of three zones, a village (*vino de pueblo*) or one of 167 *viñedos singulares*.

Rioja's whites deserve more attention. Barrel-aged Viura and Malvasía from López de Heredia (Viña Tondonia Blanco) and Murrieta (Castillo Ygay Blanco) are among the world's most singular long-lived white wines, and white plantings have doubled in twenty years.
appellations.terroir: The DOCa spans the Ebro valley from the Conchas de Haro to Alfaro, protected from the Atlantic by the Sierra de Cantabria and fed by seven tributaries from the south. Rioja Alta (cool, clay-limestone and ferrous clay, alluvial terraces), Rioja Alavesa (chalky clay-limestone terraces under the Sierra de Cantabria) and Rioja Oriental (warmer, drier, alluvial soils, Garnacha country) give three distinct climates, and altitude ranges from under 300 m to over 700 m.
appellations.nerd_note: Rioja's minimum ageing for a red Gran Reserva (two years in oak and two in bottle within five) is stricter than the national rule, but the real eccentric is López de Heredia, which still ages its Viña Tondonia whites for years in old barrels in cellars dug in 1877 and makes its own casks with an in-house cooper.

appellations.name: Ribera del Duero
appellations.grapes: Tempranillo (Tinto Fino, Tinta del País), with Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Malbec, Garnacha; Albillo Mayor for whites (at least 75%)
appellations.summary:
Ribera del Duero is the other half of Spain's red-wine aristocracy. It follows the Duero for about 115 km through four provinces (Burgos, Valladolid, Soria and Segovia), from San Esteban de Gormaz in the east to Quintanilla de Onésimo in the west, where the river runs past Vega Sicilia, Pingus, Aalto and Abadía Retuerta in a stretch nicknamed the Golden Mile. The DO dates only from 1982, when a few producers, Alejandro Fernández of Pesquera prominent among them, persuaded Madrid that the region was more than a source of rosado. Vega Sicilia, founded in 1864, had already been making legendary wine here for a century.

The wines are built on Tinto Fino, a thick-skinned local strain of Tempranillo that ripens in a short, hot season at 750 to 950 m, with nights cold enough to frost the valleys in May and September. The result is dark, firm, concentrated red, with black fruit, liquorice and minerals, often aged in French oak; the best age for decades. The DO now has about 27,300 registered hectares and roughly 250 to 300 wineries, from cooperatives to Pingus's few thousand bottles. Since the 2019 reform, white wines made mainly from Albillo Mayor are allowed, and old-style claretes, part white grapes, are being revived. Most of the vineyard lies in the province of Burgos, around Aranda, La Horra, Roa and Gumiel.
appellations.terroir: A high plateau 720 to 1,000 m up, with continental extremes, about 450 mm of rain, very cold winters and big day-night swings. Soils range from alluvial sands and gravels near the river to limestone and marl on the slopes and the chalky páramo tablelands above; the eastern Soria sector is highest and coldest.
appellations.nerd_note: Vega Sicilia's Único is released only after about a decade of ageing in vats, barrels and bottle, and some vintages wait far longer: the 1968 was released only in 1991, after 23 years.

appellations.name: Toro
appellations.grapes: Tinta de Toro (a local Tempranillo), Garnacha; Malvasía and Verdejo for whites
appellations.summary: Toro, in the province of Zamora, makes some of Spain's most powerful reds from Tinta de Toro, a thick-skinned local form of Tempranillo grown on sandy, stony soils. The wines had a reputation in medieval times, reportedly carried on Columbus's ships, but the DO dates only from 1987. In the late 1990s Vega Sicilia (Pintia), the Eguren family (Numanthia, Teso La Monja), Mariano García and the Lurton brothers arrived, attracted by ungrafted old vines and the possibility of making big, dark wines. The challenge in Toro today is freshness: earlier picking and less oak are making the wines more elegant.
appellations.terroir: A dry plateau at 600 to 750 m with about 350 to 400 mm of rain and more than 2,600 hours of sun. Sandy soils over clay and limestone, with river pebbles, allowed many ungrafted pre-phylloxera vines to survive.
appellations.nerd_note: Toro's sandy soils protected vines from phylloxera, and its old ungrafted Tinta de Toro is a reason why foreign estates came; Teso La Monja's Alma is from ungrafted vines over 100 years old.

appellations.name: Rueda
appellations.grapes: Verdejo (dominant), Sauvignon Blanc, Viura, Palomino; reds from Tempranillo since 2008
appellations.summary: Rueda, south of Valladolid, is Spain's best-selling white wine DO, and its fortunes rest on one grape: Verdejo. It used to make oxidative, sherry-like whites, *dorado* and *pálido*, aged in glass demijohns in the sun. In 1972 Marqués de Riscal, advised by Émile Peynaud, came looking for white grapes and began making fresh, cool-fermented Verdejo; the DO followed in 1980. Today Rueda has about 20,700 hectares and sells almost 900,000 hectolitres a year. The best wines, from old bush vines on stony soils around La Seca, Serrada and Rueda, can be textured and long-lived, especially when aged on lees or in barrel: Belondrade, Ossian and José Pariente show the range, and a newer *Gran Vino de Rueda* category rewards old vines and low yields.
appellations.terroir: A flat plateau at 700 to 850 m, continental, with sandy and stony alluvial soils (cascajo) rich in limestone, which give Verdejo freshness despite the heat.
appellations.nerd_note: Rueda Dorado, an oxidative fortified white aged for at least two years in glass and wood, is still defined by the DO: a living fossil of the region's medieval style.

appellations.name: Cigales
appellations.grapes: Tempranillo, Garnacha, with white Verdejo, Albillo and Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary: Cigales, just north of Valladolid along the Pisuerga, was long the city's source of claret: rosados and light reds made from a mix of red and white grapes, aged in hillside cellars. The DO keeps that tradition with its *rosado* and the old field blend style, but most wine now is red Tempranillo. About 1,900 hectares, many old bush vines, and a growing number of characterful growers.
appellations.terroir: Terraces and hills of the Pisuerga at 700 to 800 m, with sandy and stony soils over limestone, and a cold continental climate.
appellations.nerd_note: Cigales still makes its traditional rosado by blending white grapes with red, the old claret recipe; the old cellars of Mucientes and Cubillas de Santa Marta are dug into the hillsides.

appellations.name: Arlanza
appellations.grapes: Tempranillo, with Garnacha, Mencía, Cabernet Sauvignon; Albillo and Viura for whites
appellations.summary: A small, cool DO along the Arlanza river in Burgos and Palencia, around Lerma and Covarrubias, where the monks of San Pedro de Arlanza once made wine. Vineyards sit at 800 to 1,000 m, among the highest in the Duero basin, giving lighter, fresh Tempranillo. Only about 300 hectares and a few dozen growers.
appellations.terroir: High, cold and continental, with limestone and clay soils; frost is a constant risk.
appellations.nerd_note: The ruined Romanesque monastery of San Pedro de Arlanza, in the valley, is tied to Count Fernán González, the founder of Castile, who was buried there.

appellations.name: Arribes
appellations.grapes: Juan García (local), Rufete, Bruñal, Tempranillo, Mencía; Malvasía (Doña Blanca) for whites
appellations.summary: Arribes follows the Duero's gorge along the Portuguese border in Zamora and Salamanca, across the river from the Douro Superior. Terraced granite and slate slopes drop into a canyon with a surprisingly Mediterranean microclimate, where olives and almonds grow beside old vines of Juan García, a light, peppery red found almost nowhere else. A tiny, beautiful region of about 300 hectares.
appellations.terroir: Steep terraces of granite and slate above the canyon at 400 to 800 m; warm, sheltered microclimate. Fermoselle has a network of medieval cellars under the village.
appellations.nerd_note: Bruñal, a rare red grown almost only in Arribes, is genetically identical to Portugal's Alfrocheiro.

appellations.name: Tierra del Vino de Zamora
match: DO Tierra del Vino de Zamora
appellations.grapes: Tempranillo, Garnacha, Cabernet Sauvignon; Malvasía, Moscatel, Albillo, Verdejo, Palomino
appellations.summary: South of Zamora, between Toro and Salamanca, the historically named 'Land of Wine' has old bush vines on sandy and clay soils, many ungrafted. About 570 hectares and a handful of wineries, with reds of Tempranillo less heavy than Toro's.
appellations.terroir: Plateau at 650 to 800 m, continental, clay and sand soils.
appellations.nerd_note: The district has been called Tierra del Vino since the Middle Ages, a name that predates any wine law by centuries.

appellations.name: León
appellations.grapes: Prieto Picudo, Mencía; Albarín Blanco, Verdejo, Godello
appellations.summary: The DO León (originally Tierra de León) covers the plains south of the city, around Valencia de Don Juan and Valdevimbre, and is the home of Prieto Picudo, a small-berried, fresh red, and Albarín Blanco. Prieto Picudo traditionally made *rosado de aguja*, lightly fizzy, but today gives dark, savoury reds. About 1,200 hectares.
appellations.terroir: Plateau at 750 to 900 m, cold winters, alluvial terraces with stones and clay.
appellations.nerd_note: In Valdevimbre, growers still dig *cuevas*, underground cellars where rosado was traditionally made with the *madreo* method, adding whole bunches to the fermenting wine.

appellations.name: Valles de Benavente
appellations.grapes: Prieto Picudo, Tempranillo, Mencía; Verdejo, Moscatel
appellations.summary: A Vino de Calidad around the town of Benavente in northern Zamora, where the Esla, Órbigo and Tera rivers converge. Small (about 146 hectares) and focused on Prieto Picudo and Tempranillo.
appellations.terroir: Alluvial valleys at 700 to 800 m.
appellations.nerd_note: One of four Vinos de Calidad in Castilla y León, a category the 2003 law conceived as a step toward full DO status.

appellations.name: Valtiendas
appellations.grapes: Tempranillo (Tinta del País), Garnacha, Syrah
