It is known for Viña Pomal, a brand dating from 1908, and is today part of the Codorníu Raventós group.

sites.name: Bodegas Gómez Cruzado
sites.text: One of the smaller houses of the station quarter, dating from 1886. Its modern revival focuses on high-altitude Garnacha and Tempranillo from the Sierra de la Demanda foothills and old vines from the Obarenes, with village wines such as Pancrudo.

sites.name: Marqués de Riscal and the Gehry hotel
sites.text: Camilo Hurtado de Amézaga, Marqués de Riscal, built this Elciego bodega in 1858 with advice from Bordeaux, making one of the first modern wineries in Spain. His cellar El Embotellado holds bottles from 1862. Since 2006 Frank Gehry's hotel, wrapped in titanium ribbons coloured like red wine, gold mesh and silver capsules, has made the City of Wine one of Spain's most visited wineries. Riscal also pioneered Verdejo in Rueda in 1972.

sites.name: Marqués de Murrieta, Finca Ygay
sites.text: Luciano de Murrieta made the first aged Rioja for export in 1852, then founded his bodega at Finca Ygay southeast of Logroño in 1872. The estate's 300 hectares surround the restored castle. Castillo Ygay Gran Reserva Especial is one of Rioja's grand wines (the 2010 was named Wine Spectator's wine of the year in 2020), and the white Castillo Ygay is aged for years before release.

sites.name: Remírez de Ganuza
sites.text: Fernando Remírez de Ganuza, once a vineyard broker who knew every plot in the Sonsierra, founded this Samaniego winery in 1989. He famously separates the shoulders of each bunch, the ripest part, for his top wines and the tips for others. Its reserva and Trasnocho wines are among the most sought after of modern Rioja. Coordinates are approximate, for the village of Samaniego.

sites.name: Artadi
sites.text: Founded as a growers' cooperative in Laguardia in 1985 and turned into a family estate by Juan Carlos López de Lacalle. Artadi's single-vineyard wines (El Pisón, Viña El Pisón from a 1945 planting, and La Poza de Ballesteros) led modern Rioja. In 2015 Artadi announced it was leaving the DOCa, protesting at Rioja's refusal to label villages and vineyards, and since the 2016 vintage it has sold its wines outside the Rioja name.

sites.name: Viña El Pisón
sites.text: A 2.4-hectare vineyard below Laguardia planted by the López de Lacalle family in 1945, on chalky clay soils at about 520 m. Artadi's Viña El Pisón, first made in 1991, became one of the defining single-vineyard Tempranillos of modern Spain, and a test case for the argument that Rioja should be labelled by place.

sites.name: Viñedos del Contino
sites.text: Rioja's first single-estate bodega in the modern sense, founded in 1973 by CVNE and local partners on a 62-hectare loop of the Ebro at Laserna, in Rioja Alavesa. Contino pioneered a varietal Graciano and the Viña del Olivo, named after an old olive tree in the vineyard. The coordinates point to CVNE's nearby Viña Real cellar in Laserna; the estate lies just across the farmland.

sites.name: Remelluri
sites.text: A historic estate below the Toloño hermitage in Labastida, once a farm of the Monastery of Toloño (14th century), with medieval stone presses cut into rock. Jaime Rodríguez Salis bought it in 1967; his son Telmo Rodríguez returned in 2010 and turned it toward village and vineyard wines grown organically at up to 800 m.

sites.name: Bodegas Ysios
sites.text: Santiago Calatrava designed this Laguardia winery for Domecq in 2001: an undulating aluminium roof that mimics the line of the Sierra de Cantabria behind it, above a cedar facade. It belongs to Pernod Ricard and makes Tempranillo from old Alavesa vineyards.

sites.name: Laguardia
sites.text: The walled medieval capital of Rioja Alavesa, founded as a Navarrese frontier town in 1164. Beneath its streets are more than 300 old cellars and tunnels, some still used to age wine, and the town's Gothic Santa María de los Reyes church has a painted portico. Around it, chalky terraces at 600 m produce some of Rioja's finest Tempranillo.

sites.name: Sierra Cantabria
sites.text: The Eguren family's winery in San Vicente de la Sonsierra, under the cliffs of the Sierra de Cantabria. With Señorío de San Vicente and Viñedos de Páganos, they make single-vineyard Tempranillo such as Amancio and El Bosque, part of the Sonsierra's claim to some of Rioja's best north-facing sites.

sites.name: Abel Mendoza, San Vicente de la Sonsierra
sites.text: Abel Mendoza and Maite Fernández farm small plots around San Vicente de la Sonsierra and bottle single varieties, including rare whites such as Torrontés, Malvasía and Garnacha Blanca, plus field blends from old vineyards. A model for the grower movement that pushed Rioja toward village and vineyard labels.

sites.name: Finca Allende, Briones
sites.text: Miguel Ángel de Gregorio founded Finca Allende in Briones in 1995 in an 18th-century manor house. His Aurus and Calvario wines, from old vineyards around the village, helped launch modern Rioja Alta. The coordinates are for Briones village.

sites.name: Dinastía Vivanco Museum of Wine Culture
sites.text: Opened in 2004 below Briones by the Vivanco family, this is one of the largest wine museums in the world, with archaeology, presses, a corkscrew collection of thousands and art about wine from Roman mosaics to Picasso. Its garden of varieties grows more than 200 grape types.

sites.name: Monasteries of San Millán de Yuso and Suso
sites.text: Twin monasteries in the Cárdenas valley, UNESCO World Heritage Sites since 1997. Glosses in the margins of a Latin codex from here, the Glosas Emilianenses, contain the oldest written Castilian and Basque. The monks of Rioja's monasteries kept vineyards through the Middle Ages, and the area's wines are now part of Rioja Alta.

sites.name: Palacios Remondo, Alfaro
sites.text: The Palacios family winery in Alfaro, founded in 1945 and run by Álvaro Palacios since 2000. He has championed Rioja Oriental's Garnacha, especially from the slopes of Monte Yerga, and his Quiñón de Valmira, from vineyards at about 600 m, is a single-vineyard Garnacha that changed opinions of the region.

sites.name: Bodegas Riojanas, Cenicero
sites.text: Founded in 1890 by the Artacho family, with underground cellars in Cenicero, Rioja Alta. Its Monte Real brand dates from the 1920s, and its Viña Albina and Monte Real Gran Reservas are textbook classic Rioja, long aged in American oak.

sites.name: Bodegas Franco Españolas, Logroño
sites.text: Founded in 1890 by a Bordeaux merchant, Frédéric Anglade, on the banks of the Ebro in Logroño, across the river from the old town. It is a direct relic of the French phylloxera-era presence in Rioja, and its Rioja Bordón and Diamante brands are long-running classics.

sites.name: Vega Sicilia
sites.text: Founded in 1864 by Eloy Lecanda, who brought Bordeaux varieties to the Duero, and owned since 1982 by the Álvarez family. Its Único, a Tempranillo blend with Cabernet Sauvignon, is released only after about ten years of ageing, and is Spain's most legendary wine. Valbuena 5° is released after five years. The family also owns Alión (Ribera), Pintia (Toro), Macán (Rioja) and Tokaj-Oremus in Hungary.

sites.name: Dominio de Pingus
sites.text: Danish winemaker Peter Sisseck made the first Pingus in 1995 from 4 hectares of very old Tempranillo in La Horra, and Robert Parker's praise made it one of Spain's most expensive wines overnight. Now farmed biodynamically. Its second wine, Flor de Pingus, and the cooperative project PSI, which buys from old-vine growers, show the region's range. The winery is in Quintanilla de Onésimo.

sites.name: Tinto Pesquera (Alejandro Fernández)
sites.text: Alejandro Fernández, a farm-machinery maker, founded Tinto Pesquera in 1972 in Pesquera de Duero and led the campaign for the 1982 DO. Parker's famous comparison of Pesquera to Château Pétrus in the 1980s made Ribera del Duero internationally famous. Fernández later founded Condado de Haza, Dehesa La Granja (Toro) and El Vínculo (La Mancha).

sites.name: Aalto
sites.text: Founded in 1999 by Mariano García, Vega Sicilia's winemaker for 30 years, and Javier Zaccagnini, former head of the DO. Aalto and Aalto PS blend old-vine Tempranillo from across the region, from La Horra to Quintanilla. The winery near Quintanilla de Arriba sits close to the Golden Mile of the Duero.

sites.name: Bodegas Mauro, Tudela de Duero
sites.text: Mariano García founded Mauro in 1980, naming it after his father, in an old house in Tudela de Duero, just outside the Ribera del Duero boundary. Because of that the wines carry the Vino de la Tierra de Castilla y León label, proof that some of Spain's finest wines are outside the DO system. Terreus is the single-vineyard top wine. Coordinates are for Tudela de Duero.

sites.name: Abadía Retuerta
sites.text: The abbey of Santa María de Retuerta was founded in 1146. The Swiss group Sandoz (later Novartis) bought the estate in 1988 and replanted it, with the first modern vintage in 1996. The estate became a Vino de Pago in 2022 and the abbey a luxury hotel. Its Tempranillo-dominated reds came from what is one of the largest single vineyards in the Duero.

sites.name: Pago de Carraovejas
sites.text: Founded in 1987 by the restaurateur José María Ruiz, of Segovia's José María restaurant, on a south-facing hillside below Peñafiel castle. Carraovejas has grown into a group with Ossian in Rueda and Viña Meín in Ribeiro, and its high-altitude El Anejón vineyard has made a single-vineyard wine.

sites.name: Hacienda Monasterio
sites.text: An estate on the slopes above Pesquera de Duero, where Peter Sisseck has been winemaker since its founding in the early 1990s. Its Tempranillo with a little Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot shows the region's limestone in a polished style.

sites.name: Bodegas Emilio Moro
sites.text: A family winery of Pesquera de Duero, named after Emilio Moro and built into a major house by his son José Moro from the late 1980s. Its Malleolus and Malleolus de Valderramiro and Sanchomartín single-vineyard wines show old-vine Tinto Fino.

sites.name: Bodegas Alión
sites.text: Founded by the Álvarez family of Vega Sicilia in 1991 at Padilla de Duero, near Peñafiel, to make a modern Tinto Fino aged in new French oak. A counterpoint to Único's long traditional ageing, within sight of the same river.

sites.name: Peñafiel Castle and Provincial Wine Museum
sites.text: The 15th-century castle shaped like a ship's hull dominates the Duero at Peñafiel and houses the Provincial Wine Museum of Valladolid, with exhibits on the region's history and wine. Below, the Plaza del Coso and the village's underground cellars with their chimneys (*zarceras*) show how wine was kept before the cooperatives.

sites.name: Bodegas Protos, Peñafiel
sites.text: Founded in 1927 by 11 growers as the Bodega Ribera Duero, Protos (Greek for 'first') is the region's historic cooperative-turned-company. Its 2 km of tunnels under Peñafiel castle hill and its Richard Rogers-designed winery from 2008 frame the old and new Ribera.

sites.name: Aranda de Duero underground cellars
sites.text: Under the old town of Aranda lies a network of more than 7 km of medieval cellars built from the 12th to 18th centuries, kept at a constant 11 to 12 degrees. They were used to make and store wine, and some can be visited. They show how Aranda was a wine town for centuries before the DO.

sites.name: Arzuaga Navarro
sites.text: A large family estate at Quintanilla de Onésimo, founded in 1993, with a hotel and a hunting estate across 1,400 hectares of the Duero's slopes. Its Gran Arzuaga and La Planta show the Golden Mile's ripe, fleshy style.

sites.name: Numanthia
sites.text: Founded in 1998 by the Eguren family of Rioja and sold to LVMH in 2008. Its Termanthia, from ungrafted vines more than a century old, made Toro famous in the early 2000s. The coordinates are approximate, for the Valdefinjas area.

sites.name: Teso La Monja
sites.text: The Eguren family returned to Toro after selling Numanthia and in 2007 founded Teso La Monja near Valdefinjas. Its Alma comes from ungrafted pre-phylloxera Tinta de Toro, with its own small-batch top cuvée Teso La Monja among Spain's most expensive wines. Coordinates approximate.

sites.name: Bodegas Pintia, San Román de Hornija
sites.text: Vega Sicilia's Toro estate, founded in 1997 and first released in 2001. Its single Pintia wine is a polished take on Toro's power. It takes its name from Pintia, a pre-Roman Vaccaean city whose excavated site lies near Peñafiel. Coordinates are for the village of San Román de Hornija.

sites.name: Colegiata de Santa María la Mayor, Toro
sites.text: The 12th to 13th century Romanesque collegiate church of Toro, with a painted Gothic portal, overlooks the Duero plain and the vineyards of the DO. Toro's historic old town has underground wine cellars, and it was here that local wine won its medieval fame.

sites.name: Marqués de Riscal Rueda
sites.text: In 1972 Marqués de Riscal, guided by Émile Peynaud, built a winery in Rueda to make fresh white wine from Verdejo, a move that rescued the grape and set the region's modern course. The DO followed in 1980.

sites.name: Belondrade y Lurton, La Seca
sites.text: Didier Belondrade and Brigitte Lurton founded this estate in La Seca in 1994 and made a barrel-fermented, lees-aged Verdejo that showed Rueda could make ageworthy, Burgundian-style whites. Coordinates are for La Seca village.

sites.name: Ossian, Nieva
sites.text: Old ungrafted Verdejo vines on sandy soils in Nieva, Segovia, some more than 150 years old, are the basis of Ossian, founded in 2005 by Ismael Gozalo. Its wines, sold as Vino de la Tierra de Castilla y León, are among Spain's finest whites, and the project is now part of the Carraovejas group.

sites.name: Bodegas Fariña
sites.text: Manuel Fariña was a pioneer of Toro's quality revival, bottling fresher Tinta de Toro from the 1970s and helping found the DO in 1987. The family's Gran Colegiata and Primero wines remain local classics. Coordinates approximate, for the Toro winery.

sites.name: Palacio de Fefiñanes, Cambados
sites.text: A 17th-century Renaissance palace on a square in Cambados, home of one of the oldest Albariño bodegas, which has bottled its wine since 1904 and its Albariño de Fefiñanes brand since 1928. Cambados hosts the Albariño festival every August and is the capital of the Val do Salnés subzone.

sites.name: Pazo de Señorans
sites.text: A manor house (*pazo*) near Meis in the Val do Salnés, run by Marisol Bueno, a key figure in founding the DO in the 1980s. Its Selección de Añada, aged on lees for at least 30 months, proved that Albariño could age for decades.

sites.name: Do Ferreiro, Meaño
sites.text: Gerardo Méndez's family winery in Meaño, Val do Salnés, known for Cepas Vellas from an ungrafted vineyard said to be more than 200 years old. His family, including Rodrigo Méndez of Forjas del Salnés, is part of the Salnés's new generation. Coordinates are for Meaño.

sites.name: Pazo Baión
sites.text: A walled estate of about 30 hectares in Vilanova de Arousa, confiscated in the 1990s from a drug-trafficking network and later auctioned, now making a single-estate Albariño. A slice of recent Galician history in one vineyard.

sites.name: Terras Gauda, O Rosal
sites.text: The leading producer of O Rosal, the subzone at the mouth of the Miño facing Portugal, where Albariño is blended with Loureiro and Caíño Blanco. Terras Gauda helped revive Caíño Blanco. Coordinates are for O Rosal.

sites.name: Ribadavia
sites.text: The medieval capital of Ribeiro, a walled town on the Avia and Miño. Its Jewish quarter, castle of the Counts of Ribadavia and stone cellars recall the centuries when Ribeiro wine was shipped from here to England and Flanders.

sites.name: Mosteiro de San Clodio
sites.text: A Cistercian monastery in Leiro, founded in the 10th century, whose monks spread the vine through the Avia valley. Now a hotel among vineyards, it gives its name to a local wine and recalls the role of the Cistercians in Ribeiro's medieval prosperity.

sites.name: Viña Meín
sites.text: Javier Alén founded Viña Meín in Leiro in 1988, among the first to bottle Treixadura-based whites of quality, and in 2019 it joined the Pago de Carraovejas group, with Emilio Rojo's neighbouring vineyard. Coordinates approximate, near Leiro.

sites.name: Mosteiro de Santo Estevo de Ribas de Sil
sites.text: A Benedictine monastery above the Sil canyon, founded by the 10th century, with three cloisters. Its monks terraced the canyon slopes for vines. Today it is a Parador hotel, and the viewpoints nearby show the full drama of the Ribeira Sacra's terraces.

sites.name: Amandi terraces
sites.text: The Amandi subzone, on the sun-facing north bank of the Sil below Sober, holds the most spectacular terraces of the Ribeira Sacra, stepped walls on slate slopes of 80 percent or more. Its Mencía has been prized since Roman times and is the zone's most famous wine.

sites.name: Adega Algueira, Doade
sites.text: Fernando González's winery at Doade, in Amandi, where he revived old terraces and rare grapes like Merenzao, Brancellao and Caíño. Its wines helped establish the Ribeira Sacra as a fine-wine region.

sites.name: Guímaro, Sober
sites.text: Pedro Rodríguez's family winery in Amandi, which helped bring old-vine, whole-cluster Mencía from tiny terraces to world attention, with single parcel wines such as Finca Meixeman and Finca Capeliños.

sites.name: Belesar, Miño terraces
sites.text: Near Chantada, the Miño becomes a reservoir with terraced slopes plunging into it. Belesar has a Roman bridge and an annual Wine Fair of Chantada; the terraces are home to growers who harvest by boat or rail.

sites.name: Rafael Palacios
sites.text: Rafael Palacios, brother of Álvaro, settled in Valdeorras in 2004. His winery is at A Rúa, but his vineyards are high in the Bibei valley around O Bolo, where he farms Godello on granite terraces up to about 700 m. His As Sortes and O Soro are among Spain's greatest whites.

sites.name: Godeval, Xagoaza monastery
sites.text: Godeval, founded in 1986 by Horacio Fernández, one of the men of the Godello revival, is in the restored Xagoaza monastery near O Barco. Its wines were among the first varietal Godellos.

sites.name: Castelo de Monterrei
sites.text: The fortified acropolis above Verín, with a 15th-century keep and a Parador below. It controlled the frontier valley shared with Portugal's Chaves and overlooks the DO's vineyards.

sites.name: Descendientes de J. Palacios, Corullón
sites.text: Álvaro Palacios and his nephew Ricardo Pérez founded this estate in 1999, named after Álvaro's father José. From biodynamic, horse-ploughed slate slopes around Corullón they make Pétalos, Villa de Corullón and the single-vineyard La Faraona and Moncerbal, among Spain's finest reds.

sites.name: Valtuille de Abajo
sites.text: Raúl Pérez's home village, on clay and sand slopes with very old Mencía vines below Castro Ventosa. Pérez, one of Spain's most influential winemakers, makes wines all over the northwest, and his Ultreia wines come from here.

sites.name: Castro Ventosa
sites.text: A hillfort above Valtuille, identified with the Roman town of Bergidum Flavium that gave Bierzo its name. Vineyards cover its slopes, and the Pérez family's winery named after it is one of the region's oldest.

sites.name: Las Médulas
sites.text: The largest open-cast gold mine of the Roman Empire, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997, where Roman engineers collapsed mountains with water. Its red pinnacles are a reminder that Bierzo's Roman settlers also planted vines in the valley.

sites.name: Txomin Etxaniz, Getaria
sites.appellation: Getariako Txakolina / Chacolí de Getaria / Txakolí de Getaria
sites.text: A family farm (*baserri*) on the slopes above Getaria, making Txakoli for generations and one of the founding wineries of the DO in 1989. Its vineyards overlook the sea and the island of San Antón.

sites.name: Ameztoi, Getaria
sites.appellation: Getariako Txakolina / Chacolí de Getaria / Txakolí de Getaria
sites.text: A family winery in the hills between Getaria and Zarautz, run by Ignacio Ameztoi, whose rosé Rubentis and white Txakoli are among the best known abroad.

sites.name: Doniene Gorrondona, Bakio
sites.appellation: Bizkaiko Txakolina / Chacolí de Bizkaia / Txakolí de Bizkaia
sites.text: A historic farm in Bakio, the town with the Txakoli interpretation centre, making Txakoli and even a red from Hondarrabi Beltza, from old vines on the coast.

sites.name: Palacio Real de Olite
sites.text: The fairytale castle-palace of the kings of Navarre, built mainly by Charles III the Noble in the early 15th century. Olite is the capital of Navarra's wine country, home to the regional research station EVENA and the Navarra wine museum, and its royal cellars recall the court's vineyards.

sites.name: Señorío de Arínzano
sites.text: A medieval manor on a meander of the Ega with vines first planted by the Chivite family in 1988 and a winery designed by Rafael Moneo. The first Vino de Pago outside Castilla-La Mancha.

sites.name: Bodegas Otazu
sites.text: A 19th-century French-style winery and medieval tower near Pamplona, the northernmost Spanish pago. Its cellar holds contemporary art and its Chardonnays show cool northern Navarra.

sites.name: Bodegas Irache wine fountain
sites.text: Beside the Benedictine monastery of Irache on the Camino de Santiago, the Irache winery has offered free wine to pilgrims from a fountain since 1991, one of the most photographed stops on the Camino.

sites.name: Monasterio de Santa María de Veruela
sites.text: A Cistercian monastery founded in 1146 at the foot of the Moncayo, whose monks planted the vineyards of Campo de Borja. Its buildings house the Museo del Vino of the DO. The poet Gustavo Adolfo Bécquer wrote his Letters from my Cell here in 1864.

sites.name: Bodegas Borsao
sites.text: A merger of three cooperatives in 2001 created this house in Borja, which became famous in the US through importer Eric Solomon for old-vine Garnacha such as Tres Picos, from vineyards on the Moncayo slopes.

sites.name: Enate, Salas Bajas
sites.text: Founded in 1992, Enate's minimalist winery near Barbastro is known for Chardonnay, Bordeaux blends and an art collection that puts paintings by Tàpies, Saura and others on its labels.

sites.name: Viñas del Vero, Barbastro
sites.text: One of Somontano's founding modern wineries, created in 1986 and owned by González Byass since 2008. It proved that the Pyrenean foothills could make fresh Chardonnay and Gewürztraminer, and its separate Blecua estate makes the region's flagship red.

sites.name: Cartoixa d'Escaladei
sites.text: The ruins of the first Carthusian monastery in Iberia, founded in 1194 below the Montsant cliffs. For six centuries its priors governed the seven villages of the historic Priorat. Abandoned after the 1835 confiscations, it has been partly restored; the neighbouring village of Escaladei is home to Cellers de Scala Dei.

sites.name: Gratallops
sites.text: The village where the Priorat revival began in 1989. René Barbier, Álvaro Palacios, Daphne Glorian, Josep Lluís Pérez and Carles Pastrana made their first wine together here. Today Gratallops is home to Clos Mogador, Álvaro Palacios, Clos Erasmus and Costers del Siurana (Clos de l'Obac), and it is one of the 12 Vi de Vila zones.

sites.name: L'Ermita
sites.text: A steep, north-east-facing slope of llicorella below the hermitage of the Mare de Déu de la Consolació in Gratallops, planted with old Garnatxa and a little Samsó. Álvaro Palacios first made L'Ermita in 1993 and it became Spain's most expensive wine. In 2024 it was among the first three Gran Vinya Classificada of Priorat. Coordinates approximate, near the hermitage.

sites.name: Celler Álvaro Palacios
sites.text: Álvaro Palacios, son of a Rioja wine family and trained in Bordeaux, arrived in Priorat in 1989. His Gratallops winery makes Camins del Priorat, Gratallops Vi de Vila, Finca Dofí, Les Aubaguetes and L'Ermita.

sites.name: Clos Mogador
sites.text: René Barbier's estate in Gratallops, the source of the revival. Barbier, whose family came from France, and his wife Isabelle Meyer first made Clos Mogador in 1989; their son René Barbier Jr makes wine next door in Montsant (Venus La Universal). Clos Mogador was among the first wines in Catalonia recognised as a single-estate Vi de Finca.

sites.name: Clos i Terrasses (Clos Erasmus)
sites.text: Daphne Glorian, from Switzerland, joined the 1989 group and makes Clos Erasmus from a steep amphitheatre of terraces in Gratallops. Its tiny production and perfect scores from American critics made it one of the cult wines of the 2000s.

sites.name: Mas Martinet
sites.text: Josep Lluís Pérez, a biologist and oenologist, joined the 1989 group with Clos Martinet. His daughter Sara Pérez now leads the estate, one of the first to look back toward fresher, more traditional Priorat. Coordinates approximate for the farmhouse.

sites.name: Mas de la Rosa, Porrera
sites.text: A steep, old-vine vineyard of Samsó and Garnatxa in Porrera, belonging to Vall Llach, the estate co-founded by the singer Lluís Llach. Listed as one of Priorat's first three Gran Vinya Classificada in 2024. Coordinates approximate.

sites.name: Tossal d'en Bou
sites.text: A high, old-vine vineyard in the Poboleda area beneath the hill of Tossal d'en Bou, farmed by Mas Doix and planted with old Samsó (Cariñena). One of Priorat's first three Gran Vinya Classificada (2024). Coordinates approximate.

sites.name: Mas Doix, Poboleda
sites.text: The Doix and Llagostera families, who had grown grapes in Poboleda for generations, started bottling in 1998. Their old-vine Carinyena wines, 1902 and Tossal d'en Bou, are among the best expressions of the grape anywhere.

sites.name: Celler Vall Llach, Porrera
sites.text: Founded in 1998 by the Catalan singer-songwriter Lluís Llach and Enric Costa in Porrera, a village of old Samsó vines. Its Mas de la Rosa is a Gran Vinya Classificada.

sites.name: Ferrer Bobet
sites.text: A modern winery on the slopes between Falset and Porrera, founded in 2002 by Sergi Ferrer-Salat and Raül Bobet, with terraced vines at around 500 m. Its Selecció Especial shows the region's finesse.

sites.name: Celler Cooperatiu de Falset
sites.text: Cèsar Martinell's first 'cathedral of wine', built in 1919 for the Falset cooperative, with parabolic arches and tall vats. Now home to the Falset Marçà cooperative and a symbol of the Priorat comarca.

sites.name: Celler de Capçanes
sites.text: A cooperative founded in 1933 that since the 1990s has made some of Montsant's best wines, and is known worldwide for Flor de Primavera, a kosher wine made under rabbinical supervision.

sites.name: Catedral del Vi, El Pinell de Brai
sites.text: The cooperative winery of El Pinell de Brai, built 1918 to 1922 by Cèsar Martinell, with a ceramic frieze by Xavier Nogués. One of the most beautiful agricultural buildings in Europe.

sites.name: Celler Cooperatiu de Gandesa
sites.text: Martinell's 1919 cooperative winery in Gandesa, with brick arches and vats, still in use. Gandesa was at the centre of the 1938 Battle of the Ebro.

sites.name: Museu del Vi, L'Espluga de Francolí
sites.text: Catalonia's wine museum is housed in the 1913 cooperative winery of L'Espluga by Pere Domènech i Roura, son of the architect of the Palau de la Música. One of the first Catalan cooperatives.

sites.name: Reial Monestir de Santa Maria de Poblet
sites.text: Founded in 1151, Poblet is a Cistercian monastery and royal pantheon of the Crown of Aragón, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1991. Its monks have long made wine, and Codorníu's Abadia de Poblet winery works the vineyards nearby.

sites.name: Castell de Raimat
sites.text: In 1914 Manuel Raventós of Codorníu bought 3,200 hectares of saline desert around this castle, irrigated it from the Urgell canal and planted vines. Raimat's 1918 winery, by Joan Rubió i Bellver, is a pioneering concrete building, and the estate is among the largest in Europe.

sites.name: Castell del Remei
sites.text: A historic estate near Penelles in the Urgell, making wine since the 18th century, with a 19th-century castle and chapel. Revived by the Cusiné family in 1982.

sites.name: Codorníu, Sant Sadurní d'Anoia
sites.text: Josep Raventós made Spain's first traditional-method sparkling wine here in 1872. Its cellars, designed by Josep Puig i Cadafalch between 1895 and 1915, were declared a national monument in 1976 and run for kilometres underground. Codorníu, owned by the Carlyle group since 2018, makes three Cavas de Paraje Calificado.

sites.name: Freixenet, Sant Sadurní d'Anoia
sites.text: Founded by the Ferrer and Sala families in the early 20th century, Freixenet became the world's biggest traditional-method sparkling producer with Cordon Negro in its black bottle. Henkell took control in 2018. Its cellars face Sant Sadurní's railway station.

sites.name: Gramona
sites.text: A family house of Sant Sadurní since 1881, famous for long-aged sparkling wines like III Lustros and Celler Batlle, and for biodynamic farming. In 2019 Gramona left Cava as a founding member of Corpinnat.

sites.name: Recaredo
sites.text: Founded in 1924 by Josep Mata Capellades in Sant Sadurní, Recaredo is known for long-aged, biodynamic brut nature and for disgorging by hand. A founding member of Corpinnat in 2019.

sites.name: Turó d'en Mota
sites.text: Recaredo's single vineyard of Xarel·lo planted in 1940 on a small hill near Sant Sadurní; its sparkling wine, aged for a decade or more on lees, is one of the great expressions of Xarel·lo.

sites.name: Raventós i Blanc
sites.text: Descendants of the Codorníu family, the Raventós of Raventós i Blanc farm the Can Codorníu estate in Sant Sadurní. In 2012 Pepe Raventós left Cava and created the Conca del Riu Anoia label for organic, single-estate sparkling wine.

sites.name: Juvé & Camps
sites.text: A family house in Sant Sadurní since 1921, whose La Capella vineyard, the Cava de Paraje Calificado with the longest ageing (over 150 months), comes from Xarel·lo vines around a chapel in Espiells.

sites.name: Familia Torres, Pacs del Penedès
sites.text: Torres was founded in Vilafranca in 1870 by Jaume Torres. Miguel A. Torres's Gran Coronas Black Label 1970, the wine now called Mas La Plana, won the Cabernet class of the 1979 Gault-Millau Wine Olympiad in Paris. The family runs estates across Spain and Chile and leads climate-change research in Catalonia.

sites.name: Vinseum, Vilafranca del Penedès
sites.text: The Museum of Wine Cultures of Catalonia, housed in the medieval palace of the Kings of Aragón in Vilafranca. Its collections show Roman amphorae, presses and the history of Penedès wine.

sites.name: Can Ràfols dels Caus
sites.text: Carlos Esteva's estate in the Garraf massif, where he planted unusual varieties in the 1980s and dug a cellar into the limestone. Its Xarel·lo and Gran Caus wines are reference points.

sites.name: Alta Alella
sites.text: A family estate in the Serralada de Marina hills above Alella, organic and known for sparkling wine from Pansa Blanca. Its Mirgin wines from the Vallcirera paraje are among the 15 Cavas de Paraje Calificado.

sites.name: Castell de Peralada
sites.text: A 14th-century castle and convent in the Empordà, with a wine museum, a summer music festival and a 2022 winery by RCR Arquitectes, Pritzker laureates. Perelada is the region's largest producer.

sites.name: Monestir de Sant Pere de Rodes
sites.text: A Benedictine monastery above the Cap de Creus, documented from the 9th century. Its monks planted the terraces that once covered the cape, abandoned after phylloxera.

sites.name: Abadal and the stone tines
sites.text: The Roqueta family's Abadal winery has led the Pla de Bages revival since 1983, championing Picapoll and Mandó. Its estate preserves *tines*, round stone vats built in the vineyards in the 19th century to ferment wine after harvest.

sites.name: Dominio de Valdepusa
sites.text: The family estate of Carlos Falcó, Marqués de Griñón, in Malpica de Tajo, held by his family for centuries. He planted Cabernet here in 1974, adopted canopy management and drip irrigation, and in 2003 the estate became Spain's first Vino de Pago. Coordinates approximate, for the Valdepusa locality.

sites.name: Valdepeñas Museo del Vino
sites.text: A museum in an early 20th-century winery in Valdepeñas, with giant earthenware *tinajas*, presses and the history of the town that supplied Madrid's taverns once the railway arrived in the 1860s.

sites.name: Tomelloso cuevas
sites.text: Tomelloso, at the centre of La Mancha, has thousands of underground cellars (cuevas) beneath its streets, with chimneys called *lumbreras*, where wine was made and stored in huge earthenware *tinajas*. It is also Spain's biggest brandy-base town.

sites.name: Molinos de Consuegra
sites.text: Twelve windmills on the Cerro Calderico ridge above Consuegra, the image of Don Quixote's La Mancha. From the ridge the view runs across a plain of vineyards, olive groves and saffron fields, the landscape that made La Mancha the largest wine region on earth.

sites.name: Comando G, Rozas de Puerto Real
sites.text: Daniel Jiménez-Landi and Fernando García founded Comando G in 2008 to save old Garnacha in the Sierra de Gredos. From their base in Rozas de Puerto Real they make La Bruja Avería, Las Umbrías, Rumbo al Norte and El Tamboril from granite slopes at 800 to 1,200 m. Coordinates are for the village.

sites.name: Bernabeleva
sites.text: An estate near San Martín de Valdeiglesias, bought in 1923 by Vicente Álvarez-Villamil and revived in 2006 by his descendants with winemaker Marc Isart. Its Garnachas from granite, such as Arroyo del Tórtolas and Navaherreros, helped launch the Gredos movement.

sites.name: Cuevas de la Villa, Requena
sites.text: Underground caves carved under Requena's medieval old town and used for wine storage for centuries. They can be visited, and the town's wine museum is in the nearby Palacio del Cid.

sites.name: Mustiguillo, Finca El Terrerazo
sites.text: Toni Sarrión founded Mustiguillo in the late 1990s near Utiel to prove that Bobal could make fine wine. His El Terrerazo estate became the Valencian Community's first Vino de Pago in 2010. Coordinates approximate.

sites.name: Casa Castillo, Jumilla
sites.text: José María Vicente's family estate in the hills west of Jumilla, with old Monastrell on chalk and sand. Its Pie Franco and Las Gravas show how fresh Monastrell can be.

sites.name: Bodegas Castaño, Yecla
sites.text: Ramón Castaño began bottling in the 1980s and his family led Yecla's move from bulk wine to export brands, with Hécula and Solanera made from old Monastrell.

sites.name: Museo del Vino de Bullas
sites.text: The DO's wine museum occupies an old family winery in the centre of Bullas, with earthenware tinajas, presses and cellars that tell the story of Monastrell in the mountains of northwest Murcia, from village cellars to the modern DO.

sites.name: Bodegas Gutiérrez de la Vega, Parcent
sites.text: Felipe Gutiérrez de la Vega, an opera lover, founded this winery in the Marina Alta in the 1970s and makes legendary Moscatel (Casta Diva) and Fondillón.

sites.name: Bodegas Enrique Mendoza
sites.text: A family estate in L'Alfàs del Pi, near Benidorm, with vineyards inland in Villena. Its Monastrell reds, Moscatel and Fondillón were among the first to make Alicante known again to critics and importers from the 1990s on.

sites.name: Primitivo Quiles, Monòver
sites.text: A family winery in Monòver that traces its roots to 1780. It keeps an old solera of Fondillón, Alicante's oxidative, unfortified wine from overripe Monastrell, aged for decades, and still sells wine from its old town-centre cellar.

sites.name: Alt de Benimaquia
sites.text: An Iberian hillfort above Dénia, dated to the 7th and 6th centuries BC, with treading floors and tanks for making wine, among the oldest evidence of winemaking in the Iberian Peninsula.

sites.name: Macharnudo
sites.text: The most famous Sherry pago, a range of albariza hills north of Jerez rising to about 135 m. Its pure white soils give finos and amontillados of power and finesse. Valdespino's Inocente comes from Macharnudo Alto, and González Byass, Domecq and Lustau have long drawn on it. Coordinates are for the hamlet of Macharnudo Alto.

sites.name: Carrascal
sites.text: A pago of albariza hills just north of Jerez, beside Macharnudo, known for powerful olorosos and amontillados. Its name comes from the *carrasca* holm oaks that once grew there. Coordinates approximate.

sites.name: Balbaína
sites.text: A large pago of albariza west of Jerez, extending toward El Puerto (Balbaína Alta and Balbaína Baja), with exposure to the Atlantic poniente. Its wines are prized for finos and manzanillas with finesse. Coordinates approximate.

sites.name: Añina
sites.text: A pago west of Jerez, on the road to Sanlúcar, with fine albariza and Atlantic exposure. Its finos are known for delicacy, and grower Willy Pérez of Bodegas Luis Pérez has championed single-pago wines from the area. Coordinates for the hamlet of Añina.

sites.name: Los Tercios
sites.text: A pago between Jerez and El Puerto de Santa María, where the albariza is strongly Atlantic-influenced. Its name is attached to some of Jerez's modern single-pago revival wines. Coordinates approximate.

sites.name: Miraflores
sites.text: One of Sanlúcar's great pagos, just south of the town, with pure albariza close to the sea. Its Palomino is especially fine for manzanilla, and the pago is named on wines from Barbadillo, Ramiro Ibáñez and others. Coordinates approximate, near the edge of town.

sites.name: Maína
sites.text: A pago east of Sanlúcar on the Loma de la Maína ridge, with albariza rich in diatom fossils. One of the pagos used by the region's new generation of growers to show differences of soil within Sanlúcar. Coordinates approximate.

sites.name: Martín Miguel
sites.text: A Sanlúcar pago on the Loma de Martín Miguel, north of the town, close to the Guadalquivir estuary and the Atlantic. Its albariza vineyards supply some of the region's single-pago manzanillas. Coordinates approximate.

sites.name: Pastrana
sites.text: A pago on the edge of Sanlúcar whose albariza gives Hidalgo La Gitana's Pastrana Manzanilla Pasada, one of the first single-pago Sherries of the modern era. Today the pago is partly built over by the town's growth. Coordinates approximate.

sites.name: Callejuela
sites.text: A pago just east of Sanlúcar, now associated with the Blanco brothers' Bodegas Callejuela, growers who began bottling their own single-pago manzanillas and vintage wines. Coordinates approximate.

sites.name: Bodegas González Byass (Tío Pepe)
sites.text: Founded in 1835 by Manuel María González Ángel next to Jerez's Alcázar, González Byass makes Tío Pepe, the world's best-selling fino, named after his uncle José. Its old town bodegas include La Concha (1869), a circular iron-roofed hall often attributed to Gustave Eiffel. Its Tío Pepe En Rama (from 2010) and Palmas series helped spark the Sherry renaissance.

sites.name: Bodegas Lustau
sites.text: Founded in 1896 by José Ruiz-Berdejo and named after his son-in-law Emilio Lustau, Lustau became known for its Almacenista series, which bottled wines from small stockholders. It belongs to the Caballero group and works out of 19th-century bodegas in the heart of Jerez.

sites.name: Bodegas Fernando de Castilla
sites.text: A small house in Jerez's old Santiago quarter, founded in 1972 and owned since 1999 by the Norwegian Jan Pettersen. Its Antique range of very old, lightly fortified wines and its focus on unfiltered bottlings made it a favourite of sommeliers.

sites.name: Bodegas Tradición
sites.text: Founded in 1998 by Joaquín Rivero, who bought old soleras to create a house selling only VOS and VORS wines, Tradición also has a collection of Spanish art, with works by Goya, Velázquez and Zurbarán.

sites.name: Sandeman, Jerez
sites.text: George Sandeman founded his firm in London in 1790, trading Port and Sherry, and bought bodegas in Jerez. The black silhouette of the Don, in a Portuguese student's cape and Spanish hat, designed in 1928, is one of the oldest wine logos.

sites.name: Bodegas Harveys
sites.text: The Bristol merchant John Harvey & Sons, founded in 1796, created Bristol Cream in the 1880s, a blend that made sweetened Sherry a British habit, and later bought its own bodegas in Jerez.

sites.name: Williams & Humbert
sites.text: Founded in 1877 by Alexander Williams and Amy Humbert, the house built one of the largest bodegas in Jerez and created Dry Sack. It is known today for its vintage (*añada*) Sherries and its old soleras.

sites.name: Bodegas Barbadillo
sites.text: Founded in 1821 by Benigno Barbadillo in Sanlúcar's upper town, Barbadillo is the largest manzanilla house, maker of Solear and of the first white table wine of the region, Castillo de San Diego (1975). Its Reliquia wines come from very old soleras.

sites.name: Bodegas Hidalgo La Gitana
sites.text: A family house founded in 1792 in Sanlúcar, run by the Hidalgo family. Its La Gitana manzanilla is one of Spain's best-known Sherries, and its Pastrana Manzanilla Pasada was among the first single-vineyard Sherries. Coordinates approximate, in the lower town.

sites.name: Delgado Zuleta
sites.text: Founded in 1744, Delgado Zuleta is the oldest manzanilla house in Sanlúcar. Its La Goya manzanilla is named after the 1920s flamenco dancer Aurora Jauffret, called La Goya.

sites.name: Bajo de Guía
sites.text: Sanlúcar's riverside beach and restaurant row at the mouth of the Guadalquivir, opposite the Doñana National Park. Magellan's expedition left from here in 1519. Here manzanilla meets its natural partners, prawns and fried fish, and the river's humid air feeds the flor in the bodegas behind.

sites.name: Bodegas Osborne, El Puerto
sites.text: Founded in 1772 in El Puerto de Santa María by Thomas Osborne Mann from Exeter, Osborne is one of Spain's oldest companies. Its black bull silhouette, created in 1956 for a brandy advertising campaign, became a national symbol. Its bodegas in El Puerto age finos and old VORS wines. Coordinates approximate, for central El Puerto.

sites.name: Gutiérrez Colosía
sites.text: A family bodega on the bank of the Guadalete in El Puerto de Santa María, in a building from 1838. Its position near the river mouth, with sea breezes, gives finos with a thick flor, like a manzanilla. One of the few family-owned bodegas left in El Puerto.

sites.name: Alcázar de Jerez
sites.text: The 12th-century Almohad fortress of Sherish, with a mosque, Arab baths and a garden, beside González Byass's bodegas. It is a reminder of the Moorish name that gave Sherry its own.

sites.name: Castillo de Doña Blanca
sites.text: An archaeological site near El Puerto de Santa María, a Phoenician town from the 8th century BC. A stone winepress found on the nearby hill of Las Cumbres, from around the 4th to 3rd century BC, is among the oldest in western Europe, proof of wine made here long before Rome.

sites.name: Consejo Regulador Jerez-Xérès-Sherry
sites.text: The headquarters of the Consejo Regulador, which since the 1930s has regulated Sherry, Manzanilla and Brandy de Jerez and certifies VOS and VORS wines. Its building in Jerez has a visitor centre and a collection of historic barrels.

sites.name: Bodegas Alvear, Montilla
sites.text: Founded in 1729, Alvear is one of the oldest wineries in Spain. Its fino C.B. and its old PX soleras, some started in the 19th century, are references for Montilla-Moriles.

sites.name: Pérez Barquero, Montilla
sites.text: Founded in 1905, Pérez Barquero has long supplied old Montilla wines, including to Equipo Navazos, and its Gran Barquero and La Cañada PX are classics.

sites.name: Toro Albalá, Aguilar de la Frontera
sites.text: A house in Aguilar de la Frontera, in an old electricity plant, famous for very old PX such as Don PX Convento Selección, from vintages decades old. Coordinates approximate, for the town.

sites.name: Antigua Casa de Guardia, Málaga
sites.text: Málaga's oldest tavern, founded in 1840, where Málaga wine is poured from barrels and the bill is chalked on the wooden counter. A living relic of the city's sweet-wine tradition.

sites.name: Cómpeta and the Axarquía
sites.text: A white village in the Axarquía, where Moscatel grows on steep slate slopes and grapes are dried on *paseras* in the sun. Telmo Rodríguez's Molino Real, launched in 1998, and Jorge Ordóñez's wines revived Málaga's 'Mountain wine'.

sites.name: Descalzos Viejos, Ronda
sites.text: A winery in a 16th-century Trinitarian convent below Ronda's El Tajo gorge, founded in 1998, which helped show that the Serranía de Ronda could make serious mountain red wines.

sites.name: Bollullos Par del Condado
sites.text: The wine capital of Condado de Huelva, with a main street lined by old bodegas and the DO's headquarters. It makes young Zalema whites and Sherry-style Condado Pálido and Viejo.

sites.name: La Geria
sites.text: A protected landscape in the centre of Lanzarote where thousands of vines grow in pits (*hoyos*) dug through black volcanic ash, each sheltered by a horseshoe-shaped stone wall. Created after the Timanfaya eruptions of 1730 to 1736, it is one of the most striking vineyards on earth.

sites.name: Bodegas El Grifo
sites.text: Founded in 1775 in San Bartolomé, El Grifo is one of the oldest wineries in the Canaries and has a wine museum with old presses. Its Malvasía Volcánica wines, dry and sweet, are references for Lanzarote.

sites.name: Bodega La Geria
sites.text: A winery on the La Geria road in the heart of the hoyo vineyards. It is one of the easiest places to see how Lanzarote's vines grow in ash pits behind stone walls, and to taste dry and sweet Malvasía Volcánica made from them.

sites.name: Bodega Stratvs
sites.text: A modern winery in La Geria with its own vineyards in hoyos, making Malvasía Volcánica, Diego (the local name for Vijariego) and Listán Negro wines. Its terrace looks out over one of the most photographed stretches of the ash-covered vineyard.

sites.name: Suertes del Marqués, La Orotava
sites.text: Jonatan García's estate in the Orotava valley, with old ungrafted Listán Negro and Listán Blanco trained in the braided *cordón trenzado*. Its wines, from single parcels like El Esquilón and La Solana, helped launch the Canary revival.

sites.name: Casa del Vino de Tenerife, El Sauzal
sites.text: The island's wine museum, in a 17th-century farmhouse with views of Mount Teide, with exhibitions on Tenerife's wine history and tastings from all its DOs.

sites.name: Garachico
sites.text: Garachico was Tenerife's main port for exporting wine to England in the 16th and 17th centuries, until a 1706 eruption filled its harbour with lava. The historic town is a reminder of the Canary sack trade.

sites.name: Vilaflor de Chasna
sites.text: One of Spain's highest villages, at about 1,400 m on Tenerife's south slopes, surrounded by vineyards on pumice soil that climb even higher. A centre of Abona's high-altitude Listán Blanco.

sites.name: Bodegas Teneguía, Fuencaliente
sites.text: In Fuencaliente, at the southern tip of La Palma near the Teneguía volcano (1971 eruption), this winery makes sweet Malvasía and Listán, from vineyards on fresh volcanic ash.

sites.name: Caldera de Bandama
sites.text: A volcanic crater near Las Palmas, about 1 km wide and 200 m deep, with vineyards on its slopes and a farm on its floor. The area, called Monte Lentiscal, was famous for its *vino del Monte* since the 16th century.

sites.name: José L. Ferrer, Binissalem
sites.text: Founded in 1931 in Binissalem, José L. Ferrer is Mallorca's oldest and largest winery, keeper of Manto Negro and Callet, and a pioneer of the DO.

sites.name: Ànima Negra, Felanitx
sites.text: Founded in 1994 by friends from Felanitx in an old farmhouse, Ànima Negra put Callet, Mallorca's native red, on the international wine map. Coordinates are for Felanitx.
